This is a per-key fixed cooldown, the simplest form of rate limiting. The map can grow forever, so a real service would also expire old entries.
complexity: O(1) per call, O(distinct messages) space
solution: function runLogger(ops,args){const next=new Map();return ops.map((op,i)=>{if(op!=='shouldPrintMessage')return null;const [t,msg]=args[i];if(next.has(msg)&&t<next.get(msg))return false;next.set(msg,t+10);return true;});}
followups: Allow N prints per message per window (a true rate limiter).
How would you bound memory?
How would this work across many servers?

title: Design Hit Counter
statement: Design a HitCounter that counts hits in the past 300 seconds (a hit at time t is counted for times t+1 up to t+299, that is, a hit is counted at time T if T - 300 < t <= T). hit(timestamp) records a hit; getHits(timestamp) returns the number of hits in the past 300 seconds. Timestamps are non-decreasing. Input: operation names and argument lists. Return null for the constructor and hit, and the count for getHits.
hint: Hits come in time order, so old hits are always at the front. Use a queue and drop expired hits.
approach: This is a sliding-window log, the same idea as a sliding-window rate limiter. Keep a queue of hit timestamps. On getHits(T), pop from the front while the timestamp <= T - 300; the queue size is the answer. Each hit is pushed once and popped once, so the amortized cost is O(1). If one second can have millions of hits, store (second, count) pairs, or a circular array of 300 buckets, to bound the memory.
complexity: O(1) amortized per operation, O(hits in window) space
solution: function runHitCounter(ops,args){const q=[];let head=0;return ops.map((op,i)=>{if(op==='hit'){q.push(args[i][0]);return null;}if(op==='getHits'){const T=args[i][0];while(head<q.length&&q[head]<=T-300)head++;return q.length-head;}return null;});}
followups: Hits per second can be huge: how do you save memory?
Hits arrive out of order.
Make it a per-user rate limiter that allows at most N requests per window.

title: Time Based Key-Value Store
statement: Design a store where set(key, value, timestamp) saves a value, and get(key, timestamp) returns the value saved with the largest timestamp <= the given timestamp, or "" if there is none. Timestamps for each key are given in increasing order. Input: operation names and argument lists. Return null for the constructor and set, and the string for get.
hint: For each key keep a list of (timestamp, value) in sorted order. Which search finds the "largest timestamp <= t"?
approach: A hash map from key to an array of [timestamp, value] pairs. Because timestamps for a key only increase, each array is already sorted, so set is just an append. For get, binary search the array for the last pair whose timestamp is <= the query; return its value, or "" if none. Binary search turns a linear scan into O(log n).
complexity: set O(1), get O(log n), O(total entries) space
solution: function runTimeMap(ops,args){const m=new Map();return ops.map((op,i)=>{if(op==='set'){const [k,v,t]=args[i];if(!m.has(k))m.set(k,[]);m.get(k).push([t,v]);return null;}if(op==='get'){const [k,t]=args[i];const a=m.get(k)||[];let lo=0,hi=a.length;while(lo<hi){const mid=(lo+hi)>>1;if(a[mid][0]<=t)lo=mid+1;else hi=mid;}return lo?a[lo-1][1]:'';}return null;});}
followups: What if timestamps for a key can arrive out of order?
How would you shard this across machines?

title: Range Sum Query - Immutable
statement: Design a class NumArray that is built once from an integer array nums and then answers many queries sumRange(left, right), each returning the sum of nums[left..right] (both ends included). The array never changes after construction. Input: a list of operation names and a list of argument lists, like the other design problems. The first operation is "NumArray" with args [nums]; every other operation is "sumRange" with args [left, right]. Return a list with null for the constructor and the answer for each sumRange. Up to 10^4 elements and 10^4 queries; values fit in 32-bit integers.
hint: If you add up the numbers once from the left, then any range sum is a difference of two running totals.
approach: Build a prefix array where prefix[i] is the sum of the first i numbers (prefix[0] = 0). The sum of nums[left..right] is then prefix[right + 1] - prefix[left], because the first right + 1 numbers contain the first left numbers plus exactly the range we want. Building the array costs one pass, and every query after that is just one subtraction. Without it, each query would loop over the range, which is O(n) per query and too slow when there are many queries. The extra leading 0 in prefix removes the special case for left = 0. This works only because the array is immutable; if updates were allowed, the stored totals would all need fixing.
complexity: O(n) to build, O(1) per query, O(n) space
followups: What if the array can also be updated (a point update, then more range sums)? A Fenwick tree or segment tree gives O(log n) for both.
How would you extend this to sums over a rectangle of a 2-D matrix?
Can you answer "how many subarrays have sum k" using the same prefix idea?

title: Product of Array Except Self
statement: Given an integer array nums, return an array answer where answer[i] is the product of all elements of nums except nums[i]. You must not use division, and the algorithm should run in O(n) time. The array has 2 to 10^5 elements, values lie in [-30, 30], and every prefix or suffix product fits in a 32-bit integer.
hint: The product without nums[i] is (product of everything to its left) times (product of everything to its right).
approach: This is a prefix-product idea instead of prefix sums. In a first pass from the left, store in answer[i] the product of all elements before i (start with 1). In a second pass from the right, keep a running product of all elements after i and multiply it into answer[i]. After both passes, answer[i] equals left product times right product, which is the product of everything except nums[i]. Division would fail on zeros and is not allowed anyway. Using the output array to hold the left products means we need only O(1) extra space besides the answer. Zeros need no special handling: they simply make the products that include them zero.
complexity: O(n) time, O(1) extra space (not counting the output)
followups: How would you solve it with division, and what breaks when the array contains zeros?
What if you were asked for the sum of the other elements instead of the product?
Can you do it with a single output array and no other arrays? (Yes: that is the O(1) extra space version.)

title: Contiguous Array
statement: Given a binary array nums (only 0s and 1s), return the length of the longest contiguous subarray that has the same number of 0s and 1s. If there is none, return 0. The array has up to 10^5 elements.
hint: Treat every 0 as -1. Then "equal number of 0s and 1s" means the subarray sums to 0.
approach: Replace each 0 by -1 and keep a running balance (the prefix sum). A subarray has equally many 0s and 1s exactly when its sum is 0, which means the balance before it and the balance after it are the same value. So for each balance value we only need the first index where it appeared. When we reach an index i with a balance we have seen before at index j, the subarray (j, i] is balanced and has length i - j. Take the maximum over all i. We never update the stored first index, because the earliest one gives the longest subarray. Start the map with balance 0 at index -1 so subarrays that start at position 0 are counted.
followups: What if the array has three symbols and you need equal counts of all three? (Track a pair of differences.)
Can you return the subarray itself, not only its length?
How does this relate to "subarray sum equals k"?

title: Find Pivot Index
statement: Given an integer array nums, find the leftmost index i such that the sum of the elements strictly to the left of i equals the sum of the elements strictly to the right of i. An empty side counts as sum 0. Return -1 if no such index exists. The array has up to 10^4 elements with values in [-1000, 1000].
hint: If you know the total and the sum to the left, the sum to the right is total - left - nums[i].
approach: Compute the total sum of the array once. Then walk from left to right while keeping the sum of everything before the current index. At index i, the right sum is total - left - nums[i], so there is no need to compute it by scanning. If left equals that value, i is a pivot and, because we scan from the left, it is the leftmost one. Otherwise add nums[i] to left and continue. This is a prefix sum where the "suffix sum" comes for free from the total. A nested loop that recomputes both sides for every index would be O(n^2). Negative numbers do not break this, since we only compare exact equality.
followups: What if you had to return all pivot indices?
How would you do it if the array is a stream and you can only keep O(1) memory?
What changes if "left" and "right" sums must include the pivot element itself?

title: Spiral Matrix
statement: Given an m x n matrix of integers, return all its elements in spiral order: start at the top-left corner, go right along the top row, then down the right column, then left along the bottom row, then up the left column, and keep spiralling inward until every cell is visited once. 1 <= m, n <= 10.
hint: Keep four boundaries (top, bottom, left, right) and shrink one of them after you finish each side.
approach: Maintain the rectangle that has not been visited yet with four indices: top, bottom, left, right. Walk the top row left to right, then move top down by one. Walk the right column top to bottom, then move right left by one. Then, only if rows are still left, walk the bottom row right to left and move bottom up; and only if columns are still left, walk the left column bottom to top and move left right. The two guard checks matter for matrices with a single row or single column left in the middle, where walking back would visit cells twice. Each cell is output exactly once, and the loop stops when the rectangle becomes empty.
complexity: O(m * n) time, O(1) extra space
followups: Generate an n x n matrix filled with 1..n^2 in spiral order (Spiral Matrix II).
Can you do it with a direction vector and a visited set instead of four boundaries?
How would you read the spiral from the centre outward?

title: Rotate Image
statement: You are given an n x n matrix. Rotate it 90 degrees clockwise in place, without allocating another 2-D matrix. Modify the given matrix and also return it. 1 <= n <= 20.
hint: A clockwise rotation is the same as a transpose followed by reversing each row.
approach: Rotating clockwise sends the cell at (i, j) to (j, n-1-i). Do it as two simple in-place steps. First transpose: swap matrix[i][j] with matrix[j][i] for every pair above the diagonal, which turns rows into columns. Second, reverse every row. Check on one cell: (i, j) goes to (j, i) after the transpose, and reversing the row sends column i to column n-1-i, giving (j, n-1-i). Each step only swaps values inside the matrix, so extra space is O(1). The alternative is rotating four cells at a time in rings, which is also O(1) space but harder to write without off-by-one mistakes.
followups: How do you rotate counter-clockwise?
What if the matrix is m x n and not square? (You need a new matrix.)
Can you rotate by 90 degrees using four-way cell swaps in concentric rings?

title: Set Matrix Zeroes
statement: Given an m x n integer matrix, whenever a cell is 0, set its entire row and its entire column to 0. Do it in place (modify the given matrix and return it). Only the zeros that were in the original matrix count; zeros you create must not cause more rows or columns to be cleared. 1 <= m, n <= 200.
hint: Do not zero anything while you are still scanning. First record which rows and columns contain a zero.
approach: The trap is clearing as you scan: a zero you just wrote would look like an original zero and wipe too much. So use two passes. In pass one, scan the whole matrix and put the row index and the column index of every zero into two sets. In pass two, visit each cell and set it to 0 if its row or its column is in the sets. Because the decision uses only the original zeros recorded in pass one, the result is correct. This costs O(m + n) extra space. You can reduce it to O(1) by using the first row and first column of the matrix itself as the marker storage, with two extra booleans for whether those had zeros, but the logic is easier to get wrong.
complexity: O(m * n) time, O(m + n) space
followups: Can you reach O(1) extra space by storing flags in the first row and column?
What if the matrix is too large to fit in memory?
How would you do the same for "set the row and column to the cell value" instead of zero?

title: Game of Life
statement: A board has m x n cells, each alive (1) or dead (0). Every cell looks at its 8 neighbours (horizontal, vertical, diagonal) and the whole board updates at the same time: a live cell with 2 or 3 live neighbours stays alive, otherwise it dies; a dead cell with exactly 3 live neighbours becomes alive. Compute the next state. Modify the board in place and return it. 1 <= m, n <= 25.
hint: All cells must change "at once". Store the next state in a spare bit of each cell so the old state stays readable.
approach: If you overwrite a cell right away, its neighbours later see the new value instead of the old one, which is wrong. A copy of the board fixes it but uses O(m*n) space. To stay in place, use two bits per cell: bit 0 holds the current state and bit 1 will hold the next state. In the first pass, count live neighbours by reading only bit 0 (value & 1), decide the next state from the rules, and if the cell should be alive set bit 1 (value |= 2). In the second pass shift every cell right by one bit, so the next state becomes the current one. Every decision in pass one uses only old states, so the update is simultaneous.
complexity: O(m * n) time, O(1) extra space
followups: The board is infinite. How would you represent it and compute the next generation? (Keep only the set of live cells.)
If the board is huge and mostly empty, how can you avoid scanning every cell?
How would you detect when the game reaches a repeating state?

title: 01 Matrix
statement: Given an m x n binary matrix mat that contains at least one 0, return a matrix of the same size where each cell holds the distance to the nearest 0. Distance is the number of steps between cells that share a side (up, down, left, right). 1 <= m, n <= 10^4 with m * n <= 10^4.
hint: Do not search from every 1. Start one BFS from all the zeros at the same time.
approach: Searching outward from each 1 until a 0 is found repeats a lot of work. Reverse the view: all zeros have distance 0, and the answer for any other cell is one more than the smallest answer among its neighbours. A multi-source BFS computes exactly that. Put every zero cell into the queue with distance 0 and mark every 1 as unvisited. Pop a cell and look at its four neighbours; each unvisited neighbour gets distance + 1 and enters the queue. Because BFS processes cells in increasing distance order, the first time a cell is reached is by its nearest zero, so that distance is final. Each cell enters the queue once, which gives linear time.
complexity: O(m * n) time, O(m * n) space
followups: Solve it with two dynamic programming sweeps (top-left then bottom-right) and compare.
What changes if diagonal moves are allowed?
What if some cells are walls that cannot be crossed?

title: Bus Routes
statement: routes[i] lists the stops of bus i; each bus travels its stops in a loop forever, so from any stop of a bus you can ride to any other stop of the same bus. You start at stop source (not on any bus yet) and want to reach stop target. Return the minimum number of buses you must take, or -1 if it is impossible. If source equals target, the answer is 0. Up to 500 routes, up to 10^5 stops in total, stop numbers up to 10^6.
hint: The things you count are buses, not stops. Make each bus a node, or BFS over stops and expand a whole bus at once.
approach: Think of a graph where moving along a bus costs 1 no matter how many stops you ride. BFS by levels, where level k means "reachable using k buses". First build a map from each stop to the list of buses that serve it. Start with the source stop. For each stop in the current level, take every bus that serves it and has not been used yet, and mark that bus as used. Every stop of that bus is now reachable with one more bus: if one of them is the target, return the bus count; otherwise add the unseen stops to the next level. Marking buses as used is the key: each route is expanded once, so we never loop over the same long list again. If the queue empties, the target is unreachable.
followups: What if each bus had a different ticket price and you wanted the cheapest trip? (Dijkstra over stops or buses.)
What if riding between stops also took time and buses ran on a timetable?
Why is BFS over stops without marking buses as used too slow?

title: Open the Lock
statement: A lock has 4 wheels, each showing a digit 0-9 that wraps around (9 turns to 0 and 0 to 9). The lock starts at "0000". One move turns one wheel by one step up or down. Some combinations in deadends are traps: if the lock ever shows one, it is stuck and you cannot move on. Return the minimum number of moves needed to reach the string target, or -1 if impossible. Up to 500 deadends; deadends and target are 4-digit strings.
hint: Each 4-digit combination is a node; its neighbours are the 8 combinations one wheel-turn away. Deadends are nodes you must not enter.
approach: The state graph is implicit: 10^4 nodes, each connected to 8 others (4 wheels times 2 directions). Moves all cost 1, so BFS from "0000" gives the shortest number of moves. Put the deadends in a set and treat them as already visited, so the search never steps on them. If the start itself is a deadend the answer is -1; if the target is "0000" the answer is 0. For each state, build the neighbours by changing one digit to (d + 1) mod 10 or (d + 9) mod 10 and keep the ones not seen before. BFS by levels and count the level when the target first appears. If the queue runs out first, the target is blocked off and the result is -1.
followups: How does bidirectional BFS (from start and from target) cut the work?
What if the lock had k wheels and base b? What is the state count?
How would A* with a good heuristic apply here?

title: Shortest Path in Binary Matrix
statement: You get an n x n grid of 0s (open) and 1s (blocked). Find the length of the shortest path from the top-left cell to the bottom-right cell that only steps on 0 cells and may move in all 8 directions (including diagonals). The length is the number of cells on the path, start and end included. Return -1 if no path exists. 1 <= n <= 100.
hint: All steps cost the same, so a breadth-first search finds the shortest path. Remember 8 neighbours, and check if the start or end is blocked.
approach: Unweighted shortest path means BFS. If the start or the end cell is 1, answer -1 immediately. Otherwise run BFS from (0, 0) one level at a time, where the level number is the path length counted in cells (the start is length 1). For each cell, try all 8 neighbours; skip cells outside the grid, blocked cells, and cells already seen. Mark a cell as seen when you add it to the queue, not when you pop it, so that it is queued at most once. The first time we pop the bottom-right cell, the current level is the shortest length. If the queue empties without that, return -1. A 1x1 grid with 0 returns 1.
followups: How would you also return the path itself?
What if the cells had different costs? (Use Dijkstra.)
Would A* with the Chebyshev distance as heuristic help on large grids?

title: Split Array Largest Sum
statement: Split an array nums of non-negative integers into exactly k non-empty contiguous subarrays so that the largest subarray sum is as small as possible. Return that smallest possible largest sum. 1 <= nums.length <= 1000, 0 <= nums[i] <= 10^6, 1 <= k <= nums.length.
hint: Guess the largest allowed sum. Checking "can we split into at most k pieces with every piece at most this big?" is an easy greedy loop.
approach: Instead of searching for the split, search for the answer value. For a candidate limit L, a greedy check tells whether the array fits into at most k pieces: extend the current piece while its sum stays at most L, and start a new piece when adding the next number would go over. Greedy is optimal for the check, because taking as much as possible in each piece never hurts. The check is monotone: if L works, any bigger L works too. So binary search L between max(nums) (a piece must hold the biggest number) and sum(nums) (one piece). The smallest L that passes is the answer. A dynamic programming solution also exists, but it costs O(k * n^2) and is much slower.
followups: Why is the binary search valid? State the monotonic property.
Could you recover the actual split points once you have the answer?
How does this relate to painter's partition or "minimize the maximum load" problems?

title: Capacity To Ship Packages Within D Days
statement: Packages with weights weights[0..n-1] must be shipped in the given order, one ship load per day. Each day you load packages in order until adding the next one would exceed the ship capacity; the rest wait for the next day. Find the smallest capacity that ships all packages within days days. 1 <= days <= n <= 5 * 10^4, 1 <= weights[i] <= 500.
hint: For a fixed capacity you can simulate the days directly. The number of days needed only goes down as capacity grows.
approach: The answer is a capacity value, and it lies between max(weights) (we must at least carry the heaviest package) and sum(weights) (ship everything in one day). For a given capacity, simulate: add packages to the current day while the load fits, otherwise start a new day; count the days. That count never increases when capacity increases, so the predicate "ships within D days" is false up to some point and true afterwards. Binary search on capacity for the first value where the simulation uses at most D days. Each check is O(n), and there are about log2(sum) steps, so the total is fast even for 5 * 10^4 packages.
complexity: O(n * log(sum of weights)) time, O(1) space
followups: What if packages may be shipped out of order? (Becomes a bin-packing style problem.)
What is the lower bound you start the search from and why?
This looks like Koko Eating Bananas. What do the two problems share?

title: Kth Smallest Element in a Sorted Matrix
statement: You have an n x n matrix in which every row is sorted ascending and every column is sorted ascending. Return the k-th smallest value in the whole matrix, counting duplicates (so the k-th element of the sorted list of all n^2 values). 1 <= n <= 300, 1 <= k <= n^2. Aim for better than O(n^2) memory.
hint: Binary search on the value, not the position. Counting how many cells are at most x can be done in O(n) with a staircase walk.
approach: The values range from the top-left cell (smallest) to the bottom-right cell (largest). Pick a middle value mid and count how many cells are less than or equal to it. Start at the bottom-left corner: if the cell is at most mid, the whole column above it is also at most mid, so add r + 1 and move right; otherwise move up. This walk takes O(n). If the count is at least k, the answer is at most mid, so move the high bound down; otherwise the answer is larger, so move the low bound up. When low meets high, that value is the k-th smallest and it exists in the matrix, because the smallest value whose count reaches k must be a matrix element.
complexity: O(n * log(max - min)) time, O(1) space
followups: Solve it with a min-heap holding one cell per row. What is its complexity?
What if k is small compared to n? Which method wins?
What if only the rows are sorted and the columns are not?

title: Diameter of Binary Tree
statement: Given the root of a binary tree, return its diameter: the number of edges on the longest path between any two nodes. The path may or may not pass through the root. The tree is given as a level-order array with null for missing children (an empty array means an empty tree). Up to 10^4 nodes.
hint: At each node, the longest path that bends there is (depth of left) + (depth of right). Compute depths bottom-up and track the best bend.
approach: Every path has a highest node, the one where it turns. For a node, the longest path with that node on top is the depth of its left subtree plus the depth of its right subtree, measured in edges. So run a post-order DFS that returns the depth of a subtree (0 for empty, 1 + max of children otherwise) and, while doing so, updates a global best with left + right at every node. The returned value and the value we record are different: the DFS returns a single downward chain (a parent can only extend one side), while the recorded value joins two chains. The answer is the best seen over all nodes. A naive way that recomputes depth at each node is O(n^2) on a skewed tree.
complexity: O(n) time, O(h) space for the recursion
followups: How would you return the actual path, not just its length?
Adapt it to weighted edges or node values (this becomes Binary Tree Maximum Path Sum).
What if the tree is very deep? Show an iterative version.

title: Path Sum II
statement: Given a binary tree (level-order array with null) and an integer targetSum, return all root-to-leaf paths whose node values add up to targetSum. Each path is a list of node values from the root down to the leaf. A leaf is a node with no children. Return an empty list if there are none; the order of the paths does not matter. Up to 5000 nodes, values in [-1000, 1000].
hint: Walk down keeping the current path and the remaining sum. Record the path only at a leaf where the remaining sum is exactly 0.
approach: Use DFS with backtracking. Keep one shared list for the current path. When we enter a node, push its value and subtract it from the remaining target. If the node is a leaf and the remaining value is 0, copy the path into the result (the copy matters because the list keeps changing). Then recurse into the left and right children. Before returning, pop the node so the path is correct for the sibling branch. The leaf check is important: a prefix of a path that reaches the target at an inner node does not count, and negative values mean we cannot stop early when the sum goes below the target. Each node is visited once, and each result copy costs O(h).
complexity: O(n * h) time in the worst case (copying paths), O(h) extra space
followups: How would you only count the paths (Path Sum I and III) instead of listing them?
What if paths may start and end at any node, going downward? (Prefix sums with a hash map.)
Give an iterative version using an explicit stack.

title: Longest Univalue Path
statement: Given a binary tree as a level-order array with null, return the length (in edges) of the longest path in which every node has the same value. The path can start and end at any node and does not need to pass through the root. Return 0 for an empty tree or when no two connected nodes share a value. Up to 10^4 nodes, values in [-1000, 1000].
hint: It is the diameter problem again, but a child only extends the chain if its value equals the parent value.
approach: Use a post-order DFS where each call returns the longest downward chain of equal values that starts at that node (counted in edges). For a node, look at the left child: if it exists and has the same value, the left chain is (child result + 1), otherwise 0. Do the same on the right. The longest equal-valued path that turns at this node has length leftChain + rightChain, so update a global best with it. Return max(leftChain, rightChain) to the parent, since a parent can only continue one side. The result is the largest value recorded. The important step is to compare values before adding one; otherwise chains of different values would be joined. Each node is processed once.
followups: How would you count the number of nodes on the path instead of edges?
What if the values were strings or objects with a custom equality?
How is this different from Binary Tree Maximum Path Sum?

title: Binary Tree Tilt
statement: The tilt of a node is the absolute difference between the sum of all values in its left subtree and the sum of all values in its right subtree (an empty subtree has sum 0). Given a binary tree as a level-order array with null, return the sum of the tilts of all its nodes. Up to 10^4 nodes, values in [-1000, 1000].
hint: You need subtree sums at every node. Let the DFS return the subtree sum and add the tilt to a running total on the way.
approach: A post-order DFS naturally has the sum of the left and right subtrees available when it finishes a node. Let the function return the total of the subtree rooted at the node: left sum + right sum + node value. Before returning, add |left sum - right sum| to a running total, which is that node's tilt. The key point is that one traversal gives both things we need: the value passed upward (subtree sum) and the side effect (accumulated tilt). Recomputing subtree sums separately for each node would turn the solution into O(n^2) on a skewed tree. An empty tree returns 0, and a leaf has tilt 0.
followups: Why can the two things (tilt and sum) not be done by a plain recursive function that returns only the tilt?
What if you also had to return the node with the largest tilt?
Rewrite it iteratively with post-order traversal.

title: Clone Graph
statement: Make a deep copy of a connected undirected graph. Nodes are labelled 1..n and the graph is given as an adjacency list: adjList[i] holds the neighbours of node i + 1 (an empty list means a single isolated node, and an empty outer list means no graph). Build the nodes from the list, clone the graph starting from node 1 so that no node object is shared with the original, and return the clone as an adjacency list of the same form. Up to 100 nodes, no self-loops or repeated edges.
hint: Keep a map from original node to its copy. When you meet a node that is already in the map, reuse the copy instead of recursing again.
approach: A graph can contain cycles, so naive recursion would never finish. Use DFS with a hash map from original node to its clone. When visiting a node, first check the map: if the clone exists, return it. Otherwise create the clone, store it in the map before looking at the neighbours (this is what breaks cycles), and then clone each neighbour recursively and append the results to the clone's neighbour list. In the end every original node has exactly one copy, and edges between copies mirror the original edges. Here we also convert the clone back to an adjacency list so it can be compared. BFS with a queue works the same way if recursion depth is a concern.
followups: Do it with BFS and compare the memory use.
What if the graph is directed and not all nodes are reachable from the start node?
How would you clone a linked list that has random pointers (same idea)?

title: Surrounded Regions
statement: A board is an m x n grid of the characters "X" and "O". A group of connected "O" cells (connected through up, down, left, right) is surrounded if none of its cells lies on the border of the board. Turn every "O" that belongs to a surrounded group into "X". Modify the board in place and return it. 1 <= m, n <= 200.
hint: Instead of finding surrounded regions, find the "O"s that are NOT surrounded: those connected to a border cell.
approach: It is easier to look for the survivors. Any "O" that touches the border, and any "O" connected to such a cell, can never be captured. So start a DFS from every "O" on the four borders and mark all cells reached with a temporary letter, say "S" for safe. After that, every remaining "O" in the grid is enclosed, so turn it into "X", and turn each "S" back into "O". This takes two linear passes plus the DFS, and the temporary mark also acts as the visited set. An explicit stack is used so that large open regions do not overflow the recursion limit. Checking every region one by one for "does it reach the border" would repeat work.
complexity: O(m * n) time, O(m * n) space for the stack
followups: Solve it with union-find, using a dummy node for "the border".
What if diagonal neighbours also count as connected?
Why must you not flip "O"s while still searching from the border?

title: Flood Fill
statement: An image is an m x n grid of integer colours. Given a starting pixel (sr, sc) and a new colour, repaint the starting pixel and every pixel connected to it through up/down/left/right moves that has the same original colour as the starting pixel. Modify the image in place and return it. 1 <= m, n <= 50.
hint: The old colour acts as the "unvisited" mark. Be careful when the new colour equals the old colour.
approach: Remember the original colour of the starting pixel. Then run a DFS (or BFS) from there: paint a pixel with the new colour and push its four neighbours that are inside the grid and still have the original colour. Painting a pixel at the moment we push it means it will not be added twice, because it no longer has the original colour. This painting is also our visited marker, so no extra set is needed. The special case is when the new colour equals the original one: nothing would ever change, and the "visited" idea breaks, because repainted pixels would look unvisited and the search would never stop. So return the image immediately in that case.
complexity: O(m * n) time, O(m * n) space for the stack
followups: Why does the algorithm loop forever if you skip the same-colour check?
How would you handle diagonal connections?
Rewrite it with BFS and compare the stack/queue memory on a large empty image.

title: Decode String
statement: An encoded string follows the rule k[text], which means the text inside the brackets is repeated k times. Rules can be nested. Given a valid encoded string s made of lowercase letters, digits, and brackets, return the decoded string. Digits only appear as repeat counts (k can have several digits, such as 12[ab]), the input is always well formed, and the decoded length is below 10^5. The encoded string has length up to 30.
hint: When you see "[", save what you have built so far and the count; when you see "]", pop them and combine.
approach: Scan the string from left to right while keeping the text built so far at the current nesting level and the number being read. A digit extends the number (so multi-digit counts work). On "[", push the current number and the current text on two stacks, then reset both: we start a fresh inner level. On a letter, append it to the current text. On "]", pop the count and the saved outer text, and set current = outerText + current.repeat(count). That replaces the whole bracket group by its expansion and returns us to the outer level. At the end, the current text is the answer. Each character is handled once, and the stacks are as deep as the nesting.
complexity: O(L) time where L is the output length, O(depth + L) space
followups: Write it recursively instead of with two stacks.
How would you decode it if the count could be zero or the input might be malformed?
What if the decoded string is too large for memory? (Stream it as a generator.)

title: Longest Valid Parentheses
statement: Given a string made only of "(" and ")", return the length of the longest substring (contiguous) that is a valid, well-formed parentheses string. Return 0 if there is none. The string has up to 3 * 10^4 characters.
hint: Store indices on the stack, not characters. The index under the top tells you where the current valid stretch begins.
approach: Keep a stack of indices, starting with -1 as a base marker that means "the position just before a valid stretch". For "(", push its index. For ")", pop the top. If the stack is now empty, this ")" had no partner, so it becomes the new base: push its index. Otherwise the current valid stretch ends at i and starts right after the new top of the stack, so its length is i - stack top; keep the maximum. The base index always sits under any unmatched "(" or ")" that blocks us, which is why subtracting the top works even when valid pieces are glued together, like "()()". A dynamic programming approach exists too, but the stack version is shorter and uses one pass.
followups: Solve it in O(1) space with two left-to-right and right-to-left counter scans.
Write the DP recurrence and compare.
How would you return the substring itself?

title: Asteroid Collision
statement: Asteroids move along a line. Each integer in asteroids is one asteroid: its absolute value is the size, a positive sign means it moves right, a negative sign means it moves left, and all move at the same speed. When two meet, the smaller one explodes; if equal, both explode; asteroids moving the same direction never meet. Return the asteroids that remain after all collisions, in their original order. Up to 10^4 asteroids, no zeros.
hint: Only a right-moving asteroid followed by a left-moving one can collide. A stack holds the survivors so far.
approach: Process asteroids from left to right with a stack of survivors. A positive asteroid is always safe at the moment it arrives, so push it. A negative asteroid moves left and can only hit the top of the stack if that top is positive. While that is the case, compare sizes: if the top is smaller, it explodes (pop) and the new asteroid keeps going; if equal, both explode (pop and stop); if the top is bigger, the new asteroid explodes (stop). If the new asteroid survives all fights, push it. After this, the stack has no positive asteroid directly below a negative one, so no more collisions are possible. Every asteroid is pushed and popped at most once, so the loop is linear.
followups: What if asteroids had different speeds? (Event-based simulation with a priority queue.)
Can you do it in place using the input array as the stack?
Why can the new asteroid never collide with something deeper than the top after the top survives?

title: Decode Ways
statement: The letters A-Z are encoded as "1" to "26" (A = 1, B = 2, ..., Z = 26). Given a string s of digits, return the number of different ways to split it into valid codes (each code with no leading zero, from 1 to 26) and decode it into letters. "06" is not a valid code. If s cannot be decoded at all, return 0. The string has 1 to 100 characters, the answer fits in 32 bits.
hint: Let ways[i] be the number of decodings of the first i characters. The last code is either one digit or two digits.
approach: Define ways[i] as the number of ways to decode the first i characters, with ways[0] = 1 (the empty prefix). The last piece of a decoding is either one character or two characters. If the last single digit is not "0", it is a valid code, so add ways[i-1]. If the last two digits form a number from 10 to 26, add ways[i-2]. These are the only two cases and they do not overlap, so the sum is exact. A zero digit can only be used as the second digit of "10" or "20", and the rule handles this automatically: its single-digit case is skipped, and a bad pair such as "30" adds nothing. The answer is ways[n]. Only the last two values are needed, so space can be O(1).
complexity: O(n) time, O(n) space (O(1) with two variables)
followups: Reduce the memory to O(1).
Decode Ways II: the character "*" can stand for any digit 1-9. How does the recurrence change?
How would you print all the decodings and not only count them?

title: Maximum Profit in Job Scheduling
statement: There are n jobs; job i runs from startTime[i] to endTime[i] and pays profit[i]. You can do one job at a time, but a job may start at the exact moment another one ends. Choose a set of non-overlapping jobs to maximise the total profit and return that profit. Up to 5 * 10^4 jobs; times up to 10^9; profits up to 10^4.
hint: Sort jobs by end time. For each job, either skip it, or take it plus the best profit among jobs that finish by its start time (found with binary search).
approach: Sort the jobs by end time and let best[i] be the maximum profit using only the first i jobs in that order. For job i, there are two choices. Skip it: the profit is best[i-1]. Take it: the profit is its own pay plus best[j], where j is the number of earlier jobs that end at or before this job's start time. Those jobs can all be combined with it safely, and because the list is sorted by end time, j can be found with a binary search over the end times. The answer is the max of the two choices, and the last entry is the final result. The sort costs O(n log n) and each binary search O(log n). A plain O(n^2) scan over all earlier jobs would be too slow for 5 * 10^4 jobs.
complexity: O(n log n) time, O(n) space
followups: Why is it enough to sort by end time and not by start time?
What if jobs could be split across several machines?
Compare this with Weighted Interval Scheduling and Non-overlapping Intervals.

title: Counting Bits
statement: Given a non-negative integer n, return an array ans of length n + 1 where ans[i] is the number of 1 bits in the binary form of i, for every i from 0 to n. Try to do it in O(n) total time, without calling a bit-count function for each number. 0 <= n <= 10^5.
hint: The number i >> 1 is smaller and has the same bits except the last one. Reuse its answer.
approach: Shifting i right by one drops its last bit, giving i >> 1, which is smaller than i, so its answer is already computed. The number of 1 bits in i is therefore the number in i >> 1 plus the last bit of i, which is i & 1. So ans[i] = ans[i >> 1] + (i & 1), with ans[0] = 0. Fill the array from 1 to n in increasing order, and each entry takes constant time. Counting the bits of every number separately would take O(n log n). Another way to see the same table is ans[i] = ans[i & (i - 1)] + 1, where i & (i - 1) removes the lowest set bit.
complexity: O(n) time, O(n) space for the output
followups: Show the version based on i & (i - 1).
Can you do it in a single pass with no extra space besides the output? (Yes, that is what this is.)
How would you count the total number of set bits from 0 to n in O(log n)?

title: Best Time to Buy and Sell Stock with Cooldown
statement: prices[i] is a stock price on day i. You may buy and sell as many times as you want, but you can hold at most one share at a time, and after you sell you must wait one full day before you can buy again (a cooldown). Return the maximum profit. Return 0 if no profit is possible. Up to 5000 days, prices up to 1000.
hint: Track three states per day: holding a share, just sold today, and resting (no share, free to buy).
approach: Use a small state machine with the best profit in each state at the end of a day. hold: we own a share; it comes from holding yesterday, or from buying today out of the rest state (profit rest - price). sold: we sold today; it comes from holding yesterday and selling at today's price. rest: we own nothing and may buy tomorrow; it comes from rest yesterday, or from sold yesterday (the cooldown day has passed). The cooldown rule is encoded by the fact that buying only starts from rest, never directly from sold. Update the three values day by day using yesterday's values (take care to use the old sold when updating rest). The answer is the best of sold and rest on the last day, since holding a share at the end is never best.
followups: What if there is a transaction fee instead of a cooldown?
What if the cooldown lasts k days?
Limit the number of transactions to at most k. How does the state change?

title: K Closest Points to Origin
statement: Given a list of points [x, y] on a 2-D plane and an integer k, return the k points closest to the origin (0, 0) by Euclidean distance. The answer may be in any order. In the tests the k-th and (k+1)-th distances are always different, so the answer is unique. 1 <= k <= points.length <= 10^4, coordinates in [-10^4, 10^4].
hint: Compare squared distances (no square root needed). Keep a max-heap of size k so the worst of your k candidates is on top.
approach: Distance order is the same as squared-distance order, so skip the square root and keep integers. Maintain a max-heap that holds the k closest points seen so far, keyed by distance. For each new point, if the heap has fewer than k points, push it. Otherwise compare it with the root (the farthest of the current k): if the new point is closer, replace the root and sift down; if not, ignore it. After all points are processed, the heap contains exactly the k closest. Each of the n points costs O(log k), which beats sorting everything (O(n log n)) when k is small. Quickselect gives expected O(n) but changes the input order and has a bad worst case.
complexity: O(n log k) time, O(k) space
followups: Implement quickselect and discuss its average vs worst case.
What if the points arrive as a stream and you must always report the current k closest?
Why do we use a max-heap and not a min-heap of size n?

title: Find K Closest Elements
statement: Given a sorted integer array arr, an integer k, and a target x, return the k elements of arr that are closest to x, in ascending order. An element a is closer than b if |a - x| < |b - x|, and if the distances are equal, the smaller value is closer. 1 <= k <= arr.length <= 10^4, values in [-10^4, 10^4].
hint: The answer is always a contiguous window of length k. Binary search for where the window starts.
approach: Since the array is sorted, the k closest elements form a contiguous block, so we only need its starting index, which is between 0 and n - k. Binary search on that start: compare the first element of the window at mid with the element just after the window, arr[mid + k]. If x - arr[mid] is greater than arr[mid + k] - x, then the right end is closer than the left end, so the window should move right: lo = mid + 1. Otherwise (including equal distance, where the smaller left element wins) hi = mid. When lo meets hi, return arr.slice(lo, lo + k). This is much faster than a heap, which would cost O(n log k), because we use the sorted order. A two-pointer approach shrinking from both ends also works in O(n).
complexity: O(log(n - k) + k) time, O(1) extra space
followups: Solve it with a heap and explain why binary search is better here.
What if the array is not sorted?
What if there are ties and you must prefer the larger value?

title: Task Scheduler
statement: tasks is a list of uppercase letters; each letter is a task type and each task takes one time unit. The CPU runs one task per unit or stays idle. Two tasks of the same type must be at least n units apart (n idle or other tasks in between). Tasks can be run in any order. Return the minimum number of time units needed to finish all tasks. Up to 10^4 tasks, 0 <= n <= 100.
hint: The most frequent task decides the skeleton. Count how many rows of size n + 1 it forces, then check whether the other tasks fit in the gaps.
approach: Let maxFreq be the highest count of any task and countMax the number of task types that reach this count. Place the most frequent task first and then every n + 1 slots: that creates (maxFreq - 1) full frames of length n + 1, plus a final row that holds the countMax tasks which have the maximum count. That gives (maxFreq - 1) * (n + 1) + countMax slots. All other tasks fit into the gaps of this skeleton, filling idle spots. If there are so many different tasks that no idle time is needed, the answer is simply the number of tasks. So the result is the maximum of tasks.length and the formula. A max-heap simulation (always run the most frequent available task) gives the same value in O(T log 26) but needs more code.
followups: Implement it with a max-heap and a cooldown queue and compare.
Print one valid schedule, with idle slots marked.
What if tasks have different durations?

title: Generate Parentheses
statement: Given n pairs of parentheses, return all strings of length 2n made of "(" and ")" that are well formed (every "(" is closed in the right order). The order of the results does not matter. 1 <= n <= 8.
hint: Build the string one character at a time. You may add "(" while you still have some left, and ")" only if there are more "(" than ")" so far.
approach: A string is valid exactly when, at every prefix, the number of ")" never exceeds the number of "(", and the totals are both n. So build the string left to right with a backtracking function that tracks how many opens and closes were used. Add "(" if opens < n. Add ")" if closes < opens. When the length reaches 2n, store the string. Because we never take a step that could make the prefix invalid, there are no dead ends: every branch we explore leads to a valid answer, and no string is made twice. The number of results is the n-th Catalan number (14 for n = 4), so the time is dominated by the output size. Brute force over all 2^(2n) strings and filtering is much slower.
complexity: O(Catalan(n) * n) time, O(n) recursion depth
followups: How many results are there for n pairs, and why?
Generate valid strings with three bracket types, "()", "[]", "{}".
Return only the k-th valid string in lexicographic order without generating them all.

title: Palindrome Partitioning
statement: Given a string s, split it into pieces so that every piece is a palindrome, and return all possible ways to do so. Each way is a list of the pieces in order. The order of the ways in the output does not matter. s has 1 to 16 lowercase letters.
hint: Choose the first piece (any prefix that is a palindrome), then solve the same problem for the rest of the string.
approach: Use DFS with a start index. At position start, try every end index from start to the end of the string. If s[start..end] is a palindrome, add it to the current list of pieces and recurse from end + 1. When start reaches the end of the string, the current list is a complete valid partition, so copy it to the result. After the recursive call returns, remove the last piece (backtrack) and try the next end. Palindromes are checked with two pointers; for longer strings you can precompute a table isPal[i][j] with dynamic programming to avoid repeated checks. The number of partitions can grow exponentially (for "aaaa..." it is 2^(n-1)), so the output size sets the lower bound for time.
complexity: O(n * 2^n) time in the worst case, O(n) recursion depth
followups: Precompute a palindrome table with DP. What does it save?
Palindrome Partitioning II: find the minimum number of cuts instead of listing all partitions.
How many partitions does a string of n equal letters have?

title: Letter Combinations of a Phone Number
statement: On an old phone keypad, 2 = abc, 3 = def, 4 = ghi, 5 = jkl, 6 = mno, 7 = pqrs, 8 = tuv, 9 = wxyz. Given a string digits of characters 2-9, return every letter string that the digit sequence could represent. Return an empty list if digits is empty. The order of results does not matter. 0 to 4 digits.
hint: Choose one letter for the first digit, then recurse on the remaining digits. Think of a tree with one level per digit.
approach: Each digit gives a small set of letters, and the final strings are all ways to pick one letter per digit, which is a Cartesian product. Backtracking builds it level by level: at depth i, loop over the letters of digits[i], append the letter to the current string, and recurse to depth i + 1. When the depth equals the number of digits, we have a complete combination, so store it. Because we build a new string at every call (strings are immutable), there is nothing to undo; with a mutable list we would pop the letter after returning. The special case is an empty input, which must return [] and not [""]. The number of results is the product of the letter-set sizes, at most 4^4 = 256 here.
complexity: O(4^d * d) time for d digits, O(d) recursion depth
followups: Do it iteratively with a queue (build level by level).
What if the keypad mapping is given as an input?
How would you return only the combinations that are valid dictionary words? (Prune with a trie.)

title: Maximum Points You Can Obtain from Cards
statement: Cards in a row have points cardPoints[i]. In each of k steps you take one card from either the left end or the right end of the row. Return the maximum total points you can get after taking exactly k cards. 1 <= k <= cardPoints.length <= 10^5, points up to 10^4.
hint: The cards you leave behind are one contiguous block of length n - k in the middle. Minimise its sum.
approach: Taking k cards from the two ends is the same as leaving a contiguous block of n - k cards. The total score is the sum of all cards minus the sum of the block that stays, so maximising the score means finding the minimum-sum window of fixed length n - k. Compute the sum of the first window, then slide it one step at a time by adding the new right card and removing the old left card, tracking the smallest sum. Then answer = total - smallest window sum. When k = n, the window has length 0, its sum is 0, and the answer is the full total. The sliding window gives O(n) time. The other view (trying i cards from the left and k - i from the right with prefix sums) works too but needs more bookkeeping.
followups: Solve it with prefix sums of the left part and suffix sums of the right part.
What if you could also take from the middle? How does it change?
What if cards could have negative points?

title: Maximum Sum of Distinct Subarrays With Length K
statement: Given an integer array nums and an integer k, look at every contiguous subarray of length exactly k whose elements are all different. Return the largest sum among them, or 0 if no such subarray exists. 1 <= k <= nums.length <= 10^5, values in [1, 10^5]. (If k is larger than the array, the answer is 0.)
hint: Slide a window of length k and keep counts of the values inside it. The window is valid when the number of distinct values is k.
approach: Keep a window of exactly k elements with a running sum and a hash map from value to its count inside the window. Move the right edge one step: add the new value to the sum and to the map. When the window is longer than k, remove the element that left from the sum, and decrease its count; delete the key when the count reaches 0. Once the window has k elements, it contains k distinct values exactly when the map has k keys, so in that case compare the sum with the best so far. Every element enters and leaves once, so the whole scan is O(n). Sums can reach 10^10, which JavaScript numbers hold exactly.
followups: Instead of a count map, use a set plus a left pointer that moves until the window is distinct (variable window). Compare.
What if k is not fixed and you want the best distinct subarray of any length?
How would you also return the starting index of the best subarray?

title: Maximum Average Subarray I
statement: Given an integer array nums and an integer k, find the contiguous subarray of length exactly k with the largest average, and return that average as a number. Any answer within 10^-5 of the true value is accepted by the original problem; in the tests here the averages are exactly representable. 1 <= k <= nums.length <= 10^5, values in [-10^4, 10^4].
hint: The average is sum / k with the same k for all windows, so just find the largest window sum.
approach: All windows have the same length k, so comparing averages is the same as comparing sums. Compute the sum of the first k elements. Then slide the window one step at a time: add the element entering on the right, subtract the element leaving on the left, and keep the maximum sum seen. This update is O(1), so the full pass is O(n) instead of the O(n * k) you would get by summing each window again. Only at the end do we divide the best sum by k, which also avoids accumulating floating-point rounding errors from many divisions. Negative numbers are fine because we start from the real first window and not from 0.
followups: Why is it better to divide only once at the end?
Find the maximum average among subarrays of length at least k (binary search on the answer).
Return the starting index of the best window as well.

title: Move Zeroes
statement: Move all 0s in an integer array to its end while keeping the relative order of the non-zero elements. Do it in place with no extra array (modify nums and also return it). Up to 10^4 elements.
hint: Keep a write pointer for the next position of a non-zero value. Swap each non-zero into place as you read it.
approach: Use two pointers. The read pointer scans the array. The write pointer marks the first position that is not yet filled with a final non-zero value. Whenever the read pointer finds a non-zero element, swap it with the element at the write pointer and move the write pointer by one. The swap also pushes the zero that was at the write position towards the end. All non-zero values keep their order, because they are placed in the order they are found. When the scan ends, everything from the write pointer on is zero. A swap only happens for non-zero values, so the number of writes is small if few elements are non-zero. This is one pass with no additional memory.
followups: Minimise the number of writes. (Only write when read and write pointers differ.)
Do the same for moving all zeroes to the front.
Generalise: move all elements equal to a given value val to the end (Remove Element).

title: Valid Triangle Number
statement: Given an integer array nums, count the triples of indices (i, j, k) with i < j < k such that the three values can be the side lengths of a triangle with positive area (each pair of sides adds up to more than the third). Count by positions, so equal values at different positions are different triples. Up to 1000 numbers, values in [0, 1000].
hint: After sorting, only one inequality matters: the two smaller sides must add up to more than the largest side.
approach: Sort the array. For a triple a <= b <= c, the conditions a + c > b and b + c > a are automatically true (c is the largest), so only a + b > c needs checking. Fix the largest side c at index c from the end. Use two pointers l = 0 and r = c - 1 over the part before it. If a[l] + a[r] > a[c], then every index between l and r - 1 also works with r (those values are at least a[l]), so add r - l to the count and move r left. Otherwise a[l] is too small, so move l right. Each choice of c takes a linear sweep, so the total is O(n^2), better than the O(n^3) brute force. Zeros fail the inequality automatically.
complexity: O(n^2) time, O(1) extra space (besides sorting)
followups: Why does sorting reduce three inequalities to one?
Count the triples that form a degenerate (zero-area) triangle too.
Compare with 3Sum: what is the common two-pointers pattern?

title: Two Sum II - Input Array Is Sorted
statement: Given an array numbers sorted in non-decreasing order and a target, find two different positions whose values add up to target. Return their 1-based indices as [index1, index2] with index1 < index2. Exactly one solution exists. Use only constant extra space. 2 <= numbers.length <= 3 * 10^4, values in [-1000, 1000].
hint: Put one pointer at each end. If the sum is too big, which pointer must move?
approach: Start with l at the left end and r at the right end and look at their sum. If the sum equals the target, return the 1-based indices. If it is too small, the only way to make it larger is to move l right (a bigger left value), because r is already pointing at the largest value we still consider. If it is too big, move r left. Every move discards a position that can never be part of the answer: for example, when the sum is too small with the current r, then the value at l with any smaller-or-equal right partner is also too small. So we never skip the solution, and each step shrinks the range, giving a linear scan. A hash map solves the unsorted version, but needs O(n) space.
followups: Why is it correct to discard a pointer position at each step?
What if there can be several valid pairs and you must list them all, without repeats?
Extend it to 3Sum using this routine as the inner loop.

title: Find the City With the Smallest Number of Neighbors at a Threshold Distance
statement: There are n cities numbered 0..n-1 connected by weighted two-way roads edges[i] = [a, b, weight]. For each city, count how many other cities can be reached with a shortest path of total weight at most distanceThreshold. Return the city with the fewest such reachable cities; if several cities tie, return the one with the largest number. 2 <= n <= 100 (a single city is also accepted in tests), up to n(n-1)/2 edges, weights up to 10^4.
hint: With n at most 100 you can compute the shortest distance between every pair of cities, then just count.
approach: We need shortest distances between all pairs, and n is small, so Floyd-Warshall is the right tool. Start with dist[i][i] = 0, the edge weights for connected pairs (both directions), and infinity elsewhere. Then for each intermediate city k, for every pair (i, j), relax: dist[i][j] = min(dist[i][j], dist[i][k] + dist[k][j]). The order of loops matters: k must be the outermost loop. After that, dist holds true shortest distances. For each city count the other cities with dist <= threshold. Keep the city with the smallest count, and use "<=" when comparing so that a later (larger-numbered) city wins ties. Running Dijkstra from every city also works, but Floyd-Warshall is shorter at this size.
followups: Run Dijkstra from each city instead. When is that faster than Floyd-Warshall?
How would you detect a negative cycle with Floyd-Warshall?
Why must the intermediate vertex k be the outer loop?

title: Evaluate Division
statement: You are given equations like a / b = 2.0 as pairs equations[i] = [a, b] with values[i], where the variables are strings. Then answer queries [c, d] asking for the value of c / d. If the answer cannot be determined from the equations (a variable is unknown, or the two variables are not connected through the equations), return -1. A variable divided by itself is 1 if it appears in the equations. There is no contradiction and no division by zero. Up to 20 equations and 20 queries. In the tests all results are exactly representable in binary floating point.
hint: Each equation is two directed edges: a to b with weight v, and b to a with weight 1/v. A query asks for the product of weights along a path.
approach: Treat each variable as a node. An equation a / b = v gives an edge a -> b with ratio v and an edge b -> a with ratio 1 / v. The ratio of c / d is the product of the edge ratios along any path from c to d (the path is consistent because no contradictions exist). With at most 40 variables, we can fill a full table ratio[i][j] with the Floyd-Warshall idea, using multiplication instead of addition: for each middle node k, if ratio[i][k] and ratio[k][j] are known and ratio[i][j] is not, set ratio[i][j] = ratio[i][k] * ratio[k][j]. Set ratio[i][i] = 1 for known variables and use -1 for unknown. A query then reads the table, or returns -1 if a variable is missing. DFS or union-find with weights gives the same answers.
followups: Solve it with weighted union-find (store each node's ratio to its root).
Answer each query with a DFS/BFS instead. When is it better than the all-pairs table?
How would you detect contradictory equations such as a/b = 2 and b/a = 3?

title: Best Time to Buy and Sell Stock
statement: prices[i] is the price of a stock on day i. You may buy on one day and sell on a later day, once only. Return the largest profit you can make, or 0 if every possible trade loses money. 1 <= prices.length <= 100000, 0 <= prices[i] <= 10000.
hint: If you sell today, which earlier day would you have wanted to buy on?
approach: Scan the prices from left to right while remembering the lowest price seen so far. If you sell today, the best you can do is today's price minus that lowest earlier price, so update the best profit with this difference. Then update the lowest price. This greedy choice is safe because the best buy day for any sell day is always the minimum before it, so we never need to try all pairs. The brute force over all pairs is O(n^2); one pass with two variables is enough. If prices only go down, the best difference stays 0, which is the required answer.
followups: What if you may make as many trades as you like (but hold one share at a time)?
What if you may make at most two trades?
What if there is a fee for every trade?

title: Minimum Number of Arrows to Burst Balloons
statement: Each balloon is a horizontal segment [xstart, xend] on the x-axis. An arrow shot straight up at position x bursts every balloon whose segment contains x (ends included). Given points, a list of [xstart, xend] pairs, return the minimum number of arrows needed to burst all balloons. 1 <= points.length <= 100000, coordinates fit in a 32-bit signed integer.
hint: Sort the balloons by where they end. Where should the first arrow be shot?
approach: Sort the segments by their right end. Shoot the first arrow at the right end of the first balloon: this is the furthest right you can go while still bursting it, so it covers the most other balloons. Then walk through the rest; any balloon that starts at or before the arrow position is already burst. When a balloon starts after the arrow, shoot a new arrow at its right end and continue. The greedy choice works because moving an arrow left never helps and moving it right would miss the balloon that ends first. Sorting costs O(n log n) and the sweep is O(n).
complexity: O(n log n) time, O(1) extra space besides sorting
followups: How is this related to the interval scheduling and non-overlapping intervals problems?
What if each arrow can only burst balloons within a fixed vertical range?

title: Happy Number
statement: Start with a positive integer n and repeatedly replace it by the sum of the squares of its digits. If this process reaches 1, n is happy; if it loops forever in a cycle that does not contain 1, it is not. Return true if n is happy, else false. 1 <= n <= 2^31 - 1.
hint: The sequence either reaches 1 or repeats a value. How do you detect a repeat without storing everything?
approach: Treat "next number" as a function and the sequence as a linked list that either ends in the fixed point 1 or enters a cycle. Floyd's method uses a slow pointer that moves one step and a fast pointer that moves two steps. If there is a cycle they must meet inside it. If they meet at 1 the number is happy, otherwise it is not. This needs no hash set. The sequence cannot grow forever: for a number with d digits the next value is at most 81*d, so after a few steps the values stay small (below about 243), which guarantees a cycle or 1 quickly. A hash set of seen values also works but uses extra memory.
followups: Can you solve it with a hash set, and what is the trade-off?
Why can the sequence never grow without bound?

title: Find the Duplicate Number
statement: nums has n + 1 integers, each between 1 and n inclusive, and exactly one value appears more than once (it may appear many times). Return that value. Do not modify nums and use only O(1) extra space. 1 <= n <= 100000.
hint: Treat nums[i] as a pointer from index i to index nums[i]. What does a repeated value create in this graph?
approach: Because every value is in 1..n, each index i points to nums[i], and index 0 is never pointed to. Following pointers from index 0 must eventually enter a cycle. The cycle exists because two different indices point to the same place, which is exactly the duplicate value. So the duplicate is the entry point of the cycle. Use Floyd: move slow by one and fast by two until they meet. Then restart one pointer at index 0 and move both one step at a time; they meet at the cycle entrance, which is the duplicate. Sorting or a hash set are simpler but break the O(1) space or no-modify rule.
followups: How would you solve it with binary search on the value range?
What if the array could be modified and you only needed O(1) space?
Why does restarting one pointer at index 0 find the cycle entrance?

title: Middle of the Linked List
statement: Given a singly linked list (given here as an array of values from head to tail), return the values from the middle node to the end, as an array. If the list has two middle nodes, use the second one. The list has 1 to 100 nodes.
hint: If one pointer walks twice as fast as another, where is the slow one when the fast one finishes?
approach: Keep two pointers starting at the head. Move slow by one node and fast by two nodes each round. When fast reaches the end (fast or fast.next is null), slow has covered half the distance, so it sits on the middle. With an even number of nodes, fast runs off exactly when slow is on the second of the two middle nodes, which matches the rule. This avoids counting the length first and walking again, although that also works in two passes. Build the nodes from the array inside the function, then collect values from the slow pointer to the tail to produce the output array.
complexity: O(n) time, O(1) extra space (besides building the list)
followups: How would you find the node at one third of the list in one pass?
How does this help in merge sort on a linked list?

title: Reorder List
statement: A linked list L0 -> L1 -> ... -> Ln (given as an array of values) must be reordered to L0 -> Ln -> L1 -> Ln-1 -> L2 -> Ln-2 -> ... Return the reordered values as an array. Do it by relinking nodes, not by changing values. The list has 1 to 50000 nodes.
hint: Split the list in the middle, reverse the second half, then zip the two halves together.
approach: The target order alternates between the front and the back, so we need to walk the back half in reverse. Three simple steps do it in place. First, use slow and fast pointers to find the middle and cut the list there. Second, reverse the second half with the usual three-pointer reversal. Third, merge: take one node from the first half, then one from the reversed second half, and repeat until the second half is used up. The first half is the same size as the second or one node longer, so the merge ends cleanly. Each step is linear, giving O(n) time with no extra array. Copying nodes into an array and using two indices is easier but uses O(n) space.
complexity: O(n) time, O(1) extra space (besides building the list)
followups: How would you check if a linked list is a palindrome using the same idea?
What changes if the list is doubly linked?

title: Sort Colors
statement: nums contains only the values 0, 1 and 2 (think of red, white and blue). Sort it so that all 0s come first, then 1s, then 2s, using one pass and constant extra space and without a library sort. Return the sorted array. 1 <= nums.length <= 300.
hint: Keep three zones: finished 0s on the left, finished 2s on the right, and unknown in the middle.
approach: This is the Dutch national flag idea. Keep three pointers: low is the end of the zeros zone, high is the start of the twos zone, and i scans the unknown middle. If nums[i] is 0, swap it with nums[low], then move both low and i forward. If it is 2, swap it with nums[high] and move high back, but do not move i because the swapped-in value is not checked yet. If it is 1, just move i. Each element is looked at a constant number of times, so one pass is enough. Counting 0s, 1s and 2s and rewriting also works but needs two passes.
followups: What if there are k different colors?
Can you partition around a pivot with the same idea (quicksort partition)?

title: Largest Number
statement: Given a list of non-negative integers, arrange them so that when written one after another they form the largest possible number. Return that number as a string (it can be huge). If the result is all zeros, return "0". 1 <= nums.length <= 100, 0 <= nums[i] <= 10^9.
hint: Which of two numbers a and b should come first: compare the strings a+b and b+a.
approach: Sorting by numeric value or by plain string order fails: for 3 and 30, "3" > "30" but also for 34 and 3 the order depends on what follows. The right rule is a pairwise one: put a before b when the string a+b is larger than b+a. For example 9 vs 34: "934" > "349", so 9 goes first. This comparison is transitive, so it is a valid sort order, and the greedy argument is that swapping any adjacent pair that breaks the rule can only make the concatenation smaller. After sorting, join the strings. If the first piece is "0", all numbers are zero, so return "0" instead of "000".
complexity: O(n log n * L) time (L = digits), O(n) space
followups: Why must the comparator be transitive, and how do you argue that it is?
What if you wanted the smallest number instead?

title: H-Index
statement: citations[i] is the number of citations of the i-th paper of a researcher. The h-index is the largest h such that the researcher has at least h papers with at least h citations each. Return the h-index. 1 <= citations.length <= 5000, 0 <= citations[i] <= 1000.
hint: The answer can never be bigger than the number of papers n, so cap each citation count at n.
approach: The h-index is at most n, the number of papers, so any citation count above n can be treated as n. Make a counting array of size n + 1 where bucket c stores how many papers have exactly c citations (capped). Then walk h from n down to 0, keeping a running total of papers that have at least h citations. The first h where this total is at least h is the answer. This avoids sorting and runs in linear time. The sorting version also works: sort descending and find the last position i where citations[i] >= i + 1. Both are correct because the condition "at least h papers with at least h citations" can only become easier to satisfy as h gets smaller.
followups: What if the citations are already sorted? (Binary search gives O(log n).)
How does the h-index differ from the median citation count?

title: Wiggle Sort II
statement: Rearrange nums so that nums[0] < nums[1] > nums[2] < nums[3] > ... A valid answer always exists for the inputs here. Many answers are valid, so to make the result checkable, build it with this rule: sort the numbers, split them into a smaller half (the first ceil(n/2) values) and a larger half (the rest), then put the smaller half in descending order into positions 0, 2, 4, ... and the larger half in descending order into positions 1, 3, 5, ... Return the resulting array. 1 <= nums.length <= 50000.
hint: Interleave the two halves, but fill each half from its largest value to its smallest to keep equal values apart.
approach: After sorting, the smaller half should sit in the valleys (even positions) and the larger half in the peaks (odd positions). If we interleave them in ascending order, equal values near the median can end up next to each other, for example [1,2,2,3] gives 1,2,2,3 which breaks the strict rule. Filling each half in descending order fixes this: the copies of the median value from the small half land at the far end of the valley list, and those from the large half land at the far end of the peak list, so they are separated by other values. The key idea is to reverse the order inside each half before interleaving. Sorting costs O(n log n); a quickselect with a virtual index mapping can reach O(n) time and O(1) space.
complexity: O(n log n) time, O(n) space
followups: How can you get O(n) average time using quickselect for the median?
Why does the simple ascending interleave fail on [1,2,2,3]?

title: Pow(x, n)
statement: Compute x raised to the integer power n without using a built-in power function. x is a real number with |x| <= 100 (if n < 0, x is not 0), and n is an integer in [-2^31, 2^31 - 1]. The tests use values whose results are exactly representable in floating point.
hint: x^n = (x^(n/2))^2 when n is even. How many multiplications does that need?
approach: Multiplying x by itself n times needs up to 2 billion steps. Use exponentiation by squaring: x^n = (x^(n/2))^2 for even n, and x * x^(n-1) for odd n. Each step halves n, so only about 31 multiplications are needed. The iterative form keeps a running base that is squared each round and multiplies it into the result whenever the current lowest bit of n is 1. For a negative exponent, compute with |n| and invert the base at the start (or take 1 / result at the end). Work with a regular number for n, not a 32-bit integer operation, so that -2^31 does not overflow when you negate it.
followups: What happens with overflow when n = -2^31 if you use a 32-bit int?
How does the same idea speed up matrix power and Fibonacci?

title: Max Points on a Line
statement: points[i] = [x, y] is a distinct point on a 2D plane. Return the largest number of points that lie on one straight line. 1 <= points.length <= 300, -10000 <= x, y <= 10000.
hint: Fix one point as an anchor. Which points share a line with it? They share the same slope.
approach: Pick every point i as an anchor and look at all points j after it. Two points j and k are on the same line through i exactly when the direction from i to j equals the direction from i to k. Count how many points share each direction in a hash map and keep the largest group; adding the anchor gives the line size. Using floating-point slopes is risky, so represent the direction as the pair (dx, dy) reduced by their gcd and with a fixed sign (make dx positive, or dy positive when dx is 0). Vertical lines then get the key 0,1 with no division by zero. Total work is O(n^2) because there are n anchors and n others each.
followups: Why is using a floating-point slope dangerous here?
How does the answer change if points can repeat?

title: Multiply Strings
statement: num1 and num2 are non-negative integers written as decimal strings (no leading zeros except "0" itself). Return their product as a string. Do not convert the whole strings to integers and do not use a big-integer library. Each string has 1 to 200 digits.
hint: Digit i of one number times digit j of the other contributes to position i + j of the result.
approach: Do long multiplication like on paper, but with an array. The product of two numbers with a and b digits has at most a + b digits. Allocate that many slots. For every pair of digits num1[i] and num2[j] (counted from the left), their product lands in slot i + j + 1, and its carry goes into slot i + j. Add the product to what is already in slot i + j + 1, then split it into the digit (sum % 10) and the carry (floor(sum / 10)), which is added into slot i + j. Process pairs from the right end so carries only flow left. At the end, skip leading zeros; if everything was zero, return "0".
complexity: O(a * b) time, O(a + b) space
followups: How could Karatsuba make this faster for very long numbers?
How would you add, subtract, or divide two big numbers given as strings?

title: Find the Index of the First Occurrence in a String
statement: Given strings haystack and needle, return the index of the first place where needle appears inside haystack, or -1 if it never appears. Both strings have 1 to 10000 lowercase letters. Aim for linear time rather than checking every start position naively.
hint: When a match fails after matching k characters, the prefix you matched can tell you how far to jump back in needle.
approach: This is the classic KMP algorithm. First build the failure table of needle: lps[i] is the length of the longest proper prefix of needle[0..i] that is also a suffix of it. Then scan the haystack with a pointer k into needle. If characters match, advance both. If they differ and k > 0, set k = lps[k - 1] (the next shorter border) instead of restarting; the haystack pointer never moves back. If k reaches the needle length, the match starts at i - k + 1.
