Because both pointers only move forward (and k decreases at most as much as it increased), the total work is O(n + m). Naive matching can take O(n * m) on strings like "aaaa...ab".
followups: Can you do it with a rolling hash (Rabin-Karp), and what is the risk?
How would you find all occurrences instead of the first?

title: Repeated String Match
statement: Given strings a and b, return the smallest number of times a must be repeated (written back to back) so that b becomes a substring of the result. Return -1 if that is impossible. 1 <= a.length, b.length <= 10000, lowercase letters.
hint: How many copies of a are enough to cover b plus one extra misaligned start? Anything more cannot help.
approach: Let the repeated string be built from copies of a. To contain b, it must be at least as long as b, so start with ceil(len(b) / len(a)) copies. The match might begin in the middle of a copy, in which case one more copy is needed to cover the tail of b. So the answer, if it exists, is either q = ceil(len(b)/len(a)) or q + 1. Build the string with q copies and test for b; if it fails, add one more copy and test again; if that fails too, no number of copies works because adding more only repeats the same cyclic pattern. For the substring test use indexOf, or KMP to guarantee linear time.
complexity: O(len(a) + len(b)) time with KMP, O(len(a) + len(b)) space
followups: Why is q + 1 copies always enough?
How do you test the substring in guaranteed linear time?

title: Longest Happy Prefix
statement: A happy prefix of a string s is a non-empty prefix that is also a suffix, and is not the whole string. Return the longest happy prefix of s, or an empty string if there is none. 1 <= s.length <= 100000, lowercase letters.
hint: This is exactly the last value of the KMP failure (prefix) function.
approach: The KMP failure table stores, for each position i, the length of the longest proper prefix of s[0..i] that is also a suffix of that part. We want this value for the whole string, which is the last entry. Compute it left to right: keep k, the current border length. For each new character, while k > 0 and the character differs from s[k], fall back k = lps[k - 1]; if they match, k increases by one; store lps[i] = k. Fallback is safe because any shorter border of the current border is also a border of the string so far. Amortised, k goes up at most n times so it can go down at most n times in total. Hashing every prefix and suffix is an alternative but can collide.
followups: How do you use the same table to find the smallest period of a string?
Can you do this with a rolling hash, and when does it fail?

title: Shortest Palindrome
statement: You may add characters only at the front of the string s. Return the shortest palindrome you can get this way. 0 <= s.length <= 50000, lowercase letters.
hint: Find the longest prefix of s that is already a palindrome. What do you have to put in front for the rest?
approach: If the longest palindromic prefix of s has length p, then the remaining suffix s[p..] is the only part that needs mirroring: add its reverse in front and the result is a palindrome. Finding p by testing every prefix is O(n^2). Instead build t = s + "#" + reverse(s) and compute its KMP failure table. The last value is the longest string that is both a prefix of s and a suffix of reverse(s); a prefix of s equal to a suffix of reverse(s) is exactly a prefix that reads the same backwards, so it is the longest palindromic prefix. The separator "#" stops matches from running across the boundary. The answer is reverse(s.slice(p)) + s.
followups: How would a rolling hash solve it, and what is the failure risk?
How does Manacher's algorithm give another linear solution?

title: LFU Cache
statement: Design a cache with a fixed capacity that evicts the least frequently used key. Operations: LFUCache(capacity), get(key) returns the value or -1 and counts as a use, put(key, value) inserts or updates the key (an update counts as a use). When the cache is full and a new key arrives, first remove the key with the lowest use count; if several keys tie, remove the least recently used among them. A new key starts with count 1. Capacity can be 0 (then put does nothing). Both operations must run in O(1). Model it as runLFUCache(ops, args): ops[i] is the operation name (the first is "LFUCache" with [capacity]), args[i] is its argument list; return an array with null for constructor and put, and the result for get.
hint: Keep a map from each use count to the keys with that count, ordered by recency, and remember the current minimum count.
approach: Use three structures: a map key -> value, a map key -> count, and a map count -> ordered set of keys with that count (a JavaScript Map keeps insertion order, so the first key is the least recently used). Also track minFreq. On every use of a key, remove it from its bucket, move it to the bucket count + 1 (at the end, since it is now the most recent), and if its old bucket was empty and was the minimum, raise minFreq by one. On inserting into a full cache, take the first key in the bucket of minFreq and evict it. A brand-new key always has count 1, so minFreq is reset to 1. Every step is a hash-map operation, so each call is O(1).
followups: How would you make it thread-safe with fine-grained locking?
What changes if each entry also has an expiry time (TTL)?
Why do LFU caches often age counts over time?

title: Insert Delete GetRandom O(1)
statement: Design a set of integers supporting, in average O(1) time: insert(val) adds val and returns true if it was absent (false otherwise), remove(val) deletes it and returns true if it was present (false otherwise), and getRandom() returns a uniformly random element currently in the set (it is only called when the set is non-empty). Model it as runRandomizedSet(ops, args), where ops[0] is "RandomizedSet"; return an array with null for the constructor and the operation results otherwise. In the tests getRandom is only called when exactly one element is present, so the answer is deterministic.
hint: A hash map gives O(1) lookup but not random access; an array gives random access but slow removal. Combine them and swap on removal.
approach: Keep an array of the values and a map from value to its index in the array. Insert: if the value is in the map return false; otherwise push it to the array and record its index. getRandom: pick a random index in the array and return that element, which is uniform because every element has exactly one slot. Remove: finding the index is O(1) with the map, but deleting from the middle of an array shifts elements. Instead move the last element into the removed slot, update its index in the map, then pop the array and delete the removed value from the map. All steps are O(1) on average. Handle the case where the removed value is itself the last element.
complexity: O(1) average per operation, O(n) space
followups: How would you support duplicates (a multiset) with the same complexity?
How would you pick a random element weighted by a given weight?

title: Design Twitter
statement: Design a tiny social feed. postTweet(userId, tweetId) records a new tweet by the user; getNewsFeed(userId) returns the ids of the 10 most recent tweets in the feed, ordered from newest to oldest, where the feed contains the user's own tweets and tweets of the users they follow; follow(followerId, followeeId) and unfollow(followerId, followeeId) change who a user follows (following yourself or unfollowing someone you do not follow does nothing). Tweet ids are unique, and tweets are ordered by when postTweet was called. Model it as runTwitter(ops, args), where ops[0] is "Twitter"; return null for every operation except getNewsFeed, which returns an array.
hint: Store each user's tweets with a global timestamp, then merge the latest tweets of the people in the feed.
approach: Keep a global counter that increases with every tweet. Store, per user, a list of (time, tweetId) pairs in posting order, and per user a set of followees. To build a feed, collect the user plus all followees. For each of them take only their last 10 tweets, because no one can contribute more than 10 to the final top 10. Put these candidates together, sort them by time descending, and return the first 10 ids. A heap merge across users avoids sorting all candidates and is faster when a user follows many accounts, but the idea is the same: only the newest tweets of each person matter. Follow and unfollow are set operations in O(1).
complexity: postTweet/follow/unfollow O(1); getNewsFeed O(F * 10 log(F * 10)) for F followees
followups: How would you scale this to millions of users (fan-out on write vs. on read)?
How would you add pagination to the feed?
How would a heap-based k-way merge change the complexity?

title: All O`one Data Structure
statement: Design a counter of strings with O(1) operations: inc(key) adds one to the key's count (creating it with count 1), dec(key) subtracts one (the key is guaranteed to exist, and it is removed when its count reaches 0), getMaxKey() returns a key with the highest count and getMinKey() returns a key with the lowest count, or "" if the structure is empty. Model it as runAllOne(ops, args) with ops[0] = "AllOne"; return null for the constructor, inc and dec, and the key string for the two getters. Any key is valid when counts tie, so the tests only call getMaxKey/getMinKey when the answer is unique.
hint: Keep keys grouped in buckets by count, with buckets linked in sorted order, so the min and max buckets sit at the two ends.
approach: Use a doubly linked list of buckets sorted by count. Each bucket holds a count and the set of keys with that count. A hash map sends each key to its bucket. To increment a key, look at the next bucket: if it has count + 1 move the key there, otherwise create a new bucket right after the current one. Decrement is symmetric with the previous bucket. If a bucket becomes empty, unlink it. A sentinel head (count 0) and tail (count infinity) make edge cases uniform. The smallest count is the bucket right after head and the largest is right before tail, so both getters read one set. Everything is a pointer change or a hash operation, hence O(1).
followups: Why is a plain heap not enough for O(1) min and max?
How would you return all keys with the maximum count?

title: Next Greater Element II
statement: nums is a circular array: after the last element comes the first again. For every element, return the first strictly greater value you meet when moving forward (wrapping around if needed), or -1 if there is none. Return an array of the same length. 1 <= nums.length <= 10000, -10^9 <= nums[i] <= 10^9.
hint: Walk the array twice (indices 0 to 2n-1) and keep a stack of indices still waiting for a greater value.
approach: A monotonic stack keeps indices whose next greater value has not been found, with values in non-increasing order from bottom to top. When a new value arrives that is larger than the value at the top index, that index has found its answer: pop it and record the new value. Repeat while the condition holds, then push the new index. To handle the circular wrap, loop i over 0..2n-1 and use i % n for the value, but only push indices during the first lap. Indices left on the stack after two laps have no greater element and keep -1. Each index is pushed once and popped at most once, so the cost is O(n) despite the nested loop.
followups: How would you answer it for a non-circular array (the classic next greater element)?
Can you do it from right to left instead?

title: Online Stock Span
statement: Design a StockSpanner. Each call next(price) gives today's price and returns its span: the number of consecutive days, counting today and going backwards, on which the price was less than or equal to today's price. Model it as runStockSpanner(ops, args), where ops[0] is "StockSpanner" and the other ops are "next"; return null for the constructor and the span for each next. Up to 10000 calls, 1 <= price <= 100000.
hint: Keep a stack of (price, span) pairs. A new price can swallow the spans of all smaller or equal prices on top.
approach: The span of today equals 1 plus the spans of all the earlier days that it jumps over. Keep a stack of pairs (price, span) with strictly decreasing prices from bottom to top. For a new price, start with span 1 and, while the top price is less than or equal to it, pop that entry and add its span. Those days are all covered by today's span, and the popped entry already represents all the days before it that were smaller still, so no day is counted twice. Then push (price, span). The next call can then skip straight over today as a single block. Each price is pushed and popped at most once, giving O(1) amortised time per call, instead of scanning back day by day.
complexity: O(1) amortised per call, O(n) space
followups: What if you needed the span for a given window of the last k days only?
How is this related to the previous-greater-element problem?

title: Remove K Digits
statement: num is a string of digits representing a non-negative integer, and k is a count. Remove exactly k digits from num so that the remaining number is as small as possible, and return it as a string without leading zeros (return "0" if nothing is left or all digits are zeros). 1 <= k <= num.length <= 100000, num has no leading zeros.
hint: Going left to right, if the previous digit is larger than the current one, removing the previous digit makes the number smaller.
approach: The leftmost digits matter most, so we want them small. Scan the digits and keep a stack of kept digits. While we still may delete (k > 0) and the top of the stack is larger than the current digit, pop it: replacing a larger digit by a smaller one in the same position always gives a smaller number. Then push the current digit. After the scan, if k is still positive, the digits are in non-decreasing order, so remove the last k digits (the largest ones at the end). Finally strip leading zeros from the stack content and return "0" when it is empty. Each digit is pushed and popped at most once, so the algorithm is linear.
followups: Why is removing the larger previous digit always optimal?
How would you find the largest number after removing k digits instead?

title: Sum of Subarray Minimums
statement: For an array of integers arr, consider every contiguous subarray, take its minimum, and add all those minimums together. Return the sum modulo 1,000,000,007. 1 <= arr.length <= 30000, 1 <= arr[i] <= 30000.
hint: Instead of enumerating subarrays, count in how many subarrays each element is the minimum.
approach: Flip the problem: for each element arr[i], count the subarrays in which it is the minimum, multiply by arr[i], and sum. If left is the number of positions you can extend to the left before hitting a strictly smaller element, and right is the number of positions to the right before hitting a smaller-or-equal element, then arr[i] is the minimum of exactly left * right subarrays. Using strict on one side and non-strict on the other makes sure equal values are not counted twice. Find the previous-smaller and next-smaller-or-equal indices with a monotonic stack in O(n). The products stay below 2^53 here (30000 * 30000 * 30000), so plain numbers are safe if you reduce modulo after each addition.
followups: How would you compute the sum of subarray maximums, or the sum of (max - min)?
Why must one side use strict and the other non-strict comparison?

title: Min Stack
statement: Design a stack that supports push(val), pop(), top() and getMin(), all in O(1) time. getMin returns the smallest value currently in the stack. pop, top and getMin are only called on a non-empty stack. Model it as runMinStack(ops, args), where ops[0] is "MinStack"; return null for the constructor, push and pop, and the value for top and getMin.
hint: Along with each value, remember the minimum of everything below and including it.
approach: A normal stack already gives O(1) push, pop and top. The only difficulty is getMin after pops, because the minimum may be the element that was just removed. Solve it by storing, for each stack entry, the minimum of the stack up to and including that entry. When pushing val, the new minimum is min(val, current minimum), which is just the previous top's stored minimum. When popping, the entry and its stored minimum disappear together, so the stored minimum on the new top is again correct. getMin simply reads the top entry's stored minimum. This costs one extra number per element, and every operation touches only the top of the stack.
followups: Can you use less than one extra number per element (store only when the minimum changes)?
How would you add getMax as well?

title: Basic Calculator
statement: Evaluate an arithmetic expression given as a string containing non-negative integers, the operators + and -, parentheses, a unary minus (like "-(2+3)" or "(-2)"), and spaces. Return the integer result. You may not use eval. The expression is valid and intermediate results fit in 32-bit integers; length up to 300000.
hint: Keep a running result and the current sign; when you see "(", save both on a stack and start fresh.
approach: Without multiplication, only the sign in front of each number matters. Scan the characters keeping result (the value so far inside the current parentheses), sign (+1 or -1 for the next number) and the number being read. On a digit, extend the number. On + or -, add sign * number to result, reset the number and set the new sign. On "(", push the current result and the current sign on the stack, then reset result to 0 and sign to +1, because the parenthesised part is a fresh sub-expression. On ")", finish the pending number, then multiply the inner result by the saved sign and add the saved result. A leading unary minus works naturally because the starting result is 0. One pass, O(n).
followups: How would you add * and / with the usual precedence (see Basic Calculator II)?
How would you evaluate it recursively instead of with an explicit stack?

title: Basic Calculator II
statement: Evaluate an expression string with non-negative integers, the operators +, -, * and /, and spaces. Multiplication and division bind tighter than addition and subtraction; division of integers truncates toward zero. There are no parentheses. Return the result as an integer. You may not use eval. Length up to 300000; all values and intermediate results fit in 32-bit integers.
hint: Keep a stack of terms to be added. When you see * or /, combine immediately with the top of the stack.
approach: Split the expression into terms separated by + and -. Inside a term, * and / are applied left to right. Walk the string while remembering the operator seen before the current number (start with +). When a number ends (at the next operator or at the end of the string), apply the remembered operator: for + push the number, for - push its negative, for * pop the top and push top * number, for / pop the top and push trunc(top / number). The stack then holds the signed terms, and the answer is their sum. Using Math.trunc matters for negative stack tops, such as a term that came from a minus sign. One pass and O(n) time.
followups: How would you add parentheses (combine this with Basic Calculator)?
How would you do it in O(1) extra space by tracking the last term only?

title: Find First and Last Position of Element in Sorted Array
statement: nums is sorted in non-decreasing order. Return [first, last], the first and last index where target appears, or [-1, -1] if it is absent. The solution must run in O(log n). 0 <= nums.length <= 100000.
hint: Run the same binary search twice: once for the leftmost position, once for the rightmost.
approach: A standard binary search stops as soon as it finds target, which could be any copy. Instead make it find a boundary. For the left boundary, search for the first index whose value is at least target: keep lo and hi, and when nums[mid] >= target move hi to mid, otherwise lo to mid + 1. For the right boundary, search for the first index whose value is greater than target and subtract one. If the left boundary is out of range or its value is not target, the target is absent and we return [-1, -1]. Each search halves the interval, so there are two logarithmic searches rather than a linear scan outward from a found position, which would be O(n) with many duplicates.
followups: How would you count occurrences of target in O(log n)?
Why does searching for target + 1 work for integers but not for floats?

title: Find Peak Element
statement: A peak is an element strictly greater than its neighbours; treat the positions before the first and after the last element as negative infinity. Given nums where adjacent elements are different, return the index of a peak in O(log n) time. Any peak is accepted in general, but to make the answer checkable the test arrays all contain exactly one peak. 1 <= nums.length <= 1000.
hint: Look at nums[mid] and nums[mid + 1]. Which side must contain a peak if you move uphill?
approach: Binary search works even though the array is not sorted. Compare nums[mid] with nums[mid + 1]. If nums[mid] < nums[mid + 1], the array rises to the right, and since the right end is treated as negative infinity it must come back down somewhere, so a peak exists in (mid, hi]; move lo to mid + 1. Otherwise nums[mid] > nums[mid + 1], so the array falls to the right, and a peak exists in [lo, mid] (possibly mid itself); move hi to mid. Neighbours are never equal, so one of the two cases always applies. The interval shrinks by half every step and ends with lo == hi pointing to a peak. A linear scan is correct but O(n).
followups: What if the array has several peaks and you need all of them?
How does the idea extend to a 2D grid peak?

title: Search Insert Position
statement: nums is sorted ascending with distinct values. Return the index of target if it is present; otherwise return the index where it would be inserted to keep the array sorted. O(log n) time is required. 1 <= nums.length <= 10000.
hint: You want the first index whose value is greater than or equal to target.
approach: The answer in both cases is the lower bound: the smallest index i such that nums[i] >= target, or nums.length if every value is smaller. If target exists, that is its index; if not, inserting there keeps the order. Use a half-open interval [lo, hi) starting with hi = n. While lo < hi, take mid. If nums[mid] < target, the lower bound is to the right, so lo = mid + 1. Otherwise mid may be the answer, so hi = mid. When the loop ends lo == hi is the lower bound. Using the half-open form avoids the off-by-one errors of the closed-interval version and handles the "insert at the end" case without special code.
followups: What changes if duplicates are allowed and you want the rightmost insert position?
How does this relate to the C++ lower_bound and upper_bound?

title: Sqrt(x)
statement: Given a non-negative integer x, return the integer part of its square root (rounded down). Do not use a built-in square-root or power function. 0 <= x <= 2^31 - 1.
hint: You are looking for the largest integer r with r * r <= x. That predicate is true for small r and false for big r.
approach: The test r * r <= x is true for all r up to the answer and false after it, so binary search on r over the range 0..x works (or 0..46341 for 32-bit x). Keep lo and hi; take mid; if mid * mid <= x then mid is a valid candidate, so store it and search higher with lo = mid + 1; otherwise search lower with hi = mid - 1. The best stored candidate at the end is the floor of the square root. In JavaScript, numbers are doubles, so mid * mid is exact and cannot overflow here; in a language with 32-bit integers, compare mid <= x / mid instead. Capping hi at 46341 just shortens the search. Newton's method is a faster alternative.
followups: How would you compute the square root to a given number of decimal places?
Can Newton's method do it in fewer steps, and why?

title: Minimum Size Subarray Sum
statement: Given an array of positive integers nums and a positive integer target, return the length of the shortest contiguous subarray whose sum is at least target, or 0 if no such subarray exists. 1 <= nums.length <= 100000, 1 <= nums[i] <= 10000, 1 <= target <= 10^9.
hint: All numbers are positive, so adding on the right increases the sum and removing on the left decreases it.
approach: Because every number is positive, a window's sum grows when you extend it to the right and shrinks when you drop from the left. Move the right end one step at a time and add the new number. Whenever the window sum reaches target, record the window length, then shrink from the left as long as the sum stays at least target, recording the shorter length each time. Every shrink step is only done once per element, so left and right each move at most n times, giving linear time. This approach relies on positivity: with negative numbers shrinking might increase the sum and the window logic breaks. If the best length was never updated, return 0.
followups: What if the array can contain negative numbers? (Use prefix sums with a monotonic deque.)
How would you solve it with prefix sums and binary search in O(n log n)?

title: Find All Anagrams in a String
statement: Given strings s and p, return the starting indices of all substrings of s that are anagrams of p (same letters with the same counts, any order), in increasing order. Both strings contain lowercase letters only and have length up to 30000.
hint: Slide a window of length p.length over s and maintain letter counts instead of sorting every window.
approach: Every anagram of p has exactly the length of p, so look only at windows of that length. Count the letters of p in a 26-slot array. Then slide a window over s: when a character enters the window decrement its slot, and when one leaves increment it. Maintain a counter of how many slots are non-zero (or just compare all 26 slots, still constant work). When the window has the right length and every slot is zero, the window matches the counts of p, so its start index is part of the answer. Updating counts takes O(1) per step, so the whole scan is O(n). Sorting each window or building a map for each window would cost O(n * m log m).
followups: How would you handle Unicode or a larger alphabet?
How does this change if you must also report overlapping anagram groups?

title: Permutation in String
statement: Given two strings s1 and s2 of lowercase letters, return true if some substring of s2 is a permutation of s1 (contains exactly the same letters with the same counts), otherwise false. Lengths are up to 10000.
hint: A permutation of s1 is just a window of length s1.length with the same letter counts.
approach: Two strings are permutations of each other exactly when their letter counts are equal, so we only need to find a window of s2 of length s1.length with the same counts as s1. Keep two arrays of 26 counters: one for s1 and one for the current window of s2. Fill the window with the first len(s1) characters, then slide: add the new character on the right and remove the one that leaves on the left. After every slide compare the two arrays (26 comparisons, a constant). If they are ever equal return true. If s1 is longer than s2 the answer is immediately false. The overall time is O(26 * n), which is linear in the length of s2, versus sorting every window which would be slower.
followups: How would you return the index of the first matching window?
How does this differ from checking if s2 contains s1 as a substring?

title: Max Consecutive Ones III
statement: nums is a binary array (0s and 1s) and k is an integer. You may flip at most k zeros into ones. Return the length of the longest run of consecutive ones you can obtain. 1 <= nums.length <= 100000, 0 <= k <= nums.length.
hint: Equivalent question: the longest window that contains at most k zeros.
approach: Flipping zeros inside a window is only useful if the window ends up all ones, so the question becomes: what is the longest subarray containing at most k zeros? Use a sliding window with a count of zeros inside it. Extend the right end each step and, if the new element is a zero, increase the count. While the count is greater than k, move the left end forward, decreasing the count whenever a zero leaves the window. After restoring the invariant, the window length is a candidate for the answer. Each pointer moves forward at most n times, so the algorithm is linear, and it needs no extra memory besides the counters.
followups: How would you also return the positions of the zeros to flip?
What if the array has values other than 0 and 1?

title: Remove Duplicates from Sorted Array
statement: nums is sorted in non-decreasing order. Remove the duplicates in place so each distinct value appears once, keeping their relative order. Return the array of the first k elements after the operation, where k is the number of distinct values (the original problem returns k and checks the first k slots). Use O(1) extra space. 1 <= nums.length <= 30000.
hint: Use one pointer to read and another to mark where the next distinct value should be written.
approach: Since the array is sorted, equal values are next to each other, so a value is a duplicate exactly when it equals the last value we kept. Keep a write index w for the next free slot (start at 1, because the first element is always kept). Scan with a read index r from 1: if nums[r] differs from nums[w - 1], copy it to nums[w] and increase w. At the end, w is k and the first k slots hold the distinct values in order. Each element is read once and written at most once, so the work is linear with no extra array. Comparing with the last kept element, rather than the previous element read, makes the same loop easy to generalise to allow each value up to two times.
followups: What if each value may appear at most twice?
How would you do it for an unsorted array?

title: Merge Sorted Array
statement: nums1 has length m + n: its first m entries are sorted values and the last n entries are 0 placeholders. nums2 has n sorted values. Merge nums2 into nums1 so that nums1 becomes one sorted array of m + n values, in place, then return nums1. 0 <= m, n <= 200.
hint: Fill nums1 from the back, so you never overwrite a value you still need.
approach: If we merged from the front we would overwrite elements of nums1 that have not been used yet. The free space is at the end of nums1, so merge from the back instead. Keep three indices: i at the last real element of nums1 (m - 1), j at the last element of nums2 (n - 1) and k at the last slot of nums1 (m + n - 1). Compare nums1[i] and nums2[j], write the larger into nums1[k], and move that pointer and k backwards. When nums2 is used up, the remaining part of nums1 is already in place. If nums1 runs out first, copy the rest of nums2. This is a single pass using O(1) extra space.
followups: What if you must merge k sorted arrays?
Why does merging from the front fail without extra space?

title: Squares of a Sorted Array
statement: nums is sorted in non-decreasing order and may contain negative numbers. Return an array of the squares of each number, also sorted in non-decreasing order. 1 <= nums.length <= 10000, -10000 <= nums[i] <= 10000. Try to beat O(n log n).
hint: The largest square is at one of the two ends. Which end?
approach: Squaring makes the negative numbers positive, so the squares are no longer sorted, but they form a valley shape: big at both ends (large magnitudes) and small in the middle. The largest square is therefore either at the left end or at the right end. Use two pointers, left at 0 and right at the last index, and fill the result array from the back: compare the absolute values at the two pointers, write the square of the bigger one at the current back position, and move that pointer inward. After n steps the result is sorted. This is linear time. The simple approach of squaring everything and calling sort costs O(n log n) and ignores the sorted structure of the input.
complexity: O(n) time, O(n) space for the output
followups: What if the array is sorted by absolute value already?
How would you do it in place?

title: 3Sum Closest
statement: Given an integer array nums and an integer target, choose three different elements (by position) whose sum is as close to target as possible, and return that sum. The tests are built so the closest sum is unique. 3 <= nums.length <= 500, -1000 <= nums[i] <= 1000, -10^4 <= target <= 10^4.
hint: Sort the array, fix one element, and use two pointers on the rest like in 3Sum.
approach: Sort the array first. For each index i, treat nums[i] as the first number and look for the best pair in the remaining part to its right with two pointers: lo = i + 1 and hi = n - 1. Compute sum = nums[i] + nums[lo] + nums[hi] and update the best answer if it is closer to target. If the sum is smaller than target we need a bigger sum, so move lo right; if it is larger, move hi left; if it equals target return immediately because nothing can be closer. Sorting makes each move safe: moving lo right can only increase the sum, moving hi left can only decrease it. The cost is O(n log n) for sorting plus O(n^2) for the scans, instead of O(n^3) for trying all triples.
followups: How would you return the three indices or values instead of just the sum?
Why can you not use a hash set here as in Two Sum?

title: Binary Tree Right Side View
statement: Imagine standing on the right side of a binary tree. Return the values of the nodes you can see, from top to bottom. The tree is given as a level-order array where null marks a missing child (children of null are not listed), for example [1,2,3,null,5,null,4]. The tree has 0 to 100 nodes.
hint: The node you see at each depth is the last node of that level.
approach: From the right, at each depth you see the rightmost node of that level. A breadth-first traversal processes the tree level by level, so for every level just remember the last node processed and add its value to the answer. Implementation: put the root in a queue, and in each round take the current queue size as the number of nodes in this level; pop that many nodes, push their children left then right, and record the value of the last one popped. An alternative is a DFS that visits the right child first and records a value when it reaches a new depth for the first time. Both visit each node once, so the work is O(n), with O(w) memory for the widest level.
complexity: O(n) time, O(w) space (w = max width)
followups: How would you compute the left side view too?
How would you do it with DFS and no queue?

title: Binary Tree Zigzag Level Order Traversal
statement: Return the level-order traversal of a binary tree where the direction alternates: the first level is read left to right, the second right to left, the third left to right, and so on. The tree is given as a level-order array with null for missing children. Return an array of arrays of values. The tree has 0 to 2000 nodes.
hint: Do a normal level-by-level BFS and reverse every second level.
approach: Run an ordinary breadth-first search that handles one level at a time. For each level, collect the node values from left to right in the order they come from the queue, and also collect the children for the next level, always left child first. Then, if the level number is odd (counting from 0), reverse the collected values before adding them to the answer. The traversal order of the queue must stay left to right, otherwise the next level would be built in the wrong order, so the reversal is applied only to the output of the level. Each node is visited once and each reversal costs the size of the level, so the total time is O(n).
followups: How would you do it using a deque instead of reversing?
How would you do it with DFS and a depth parameter?

title: Minimum Depth of Binary Tree
statement: Return the minimum depth of a binary tree: the number of nodes on the shortest path from the root down to a leaf (a node with no children). An empty tree has depth 0. The tree is given as a level-order array with null for missing children. Up to 100000 nodes.
hint: Level-order search finds the first leaf as soon as it reaches one. Careful: a node with only one child is not a leaf.
approach: The shortest root-to-leaf path is found by breadth-first search, because BFS reaches nodes in order of depth: the first leaf we meet is at the minimum depth, and we can stop at once without visiting the rest of the tree. Keep the current level in a list and a depth counter starting at 1. For each node in the level, if it has no left and no right child, return the depth. Otherwise add its existing children to the next level. A recursive solution is also possible, but it must not simply take 1 + min(left, right): when one child is missing that formula would count the empty side as depth 0 and wrongly treat the node as a leaf. Time is O(n) in the worst case.
followups: Why does 1 + min(left, right) fail for a skewed tree?
When is BFS better than DFS for this problem?

title: Invert Binary Tree
statement: Mirror a binary tree: swap the left and right child of every node. The tree is given as a level-order array with null for missing children (children of null are not listed, and trailing nulls are dropped). Return the inverted tree in the same format. Up to 100 nodes.
hint: If you swap the children of the root, what do you still need to do for the two subtrees?
approach: Mirroring the whole tree means mirroring each subtree and then swapping the two children. A recursive depth-first function expresses this directly: if the node is null, return null; otherwise invert the left subtree, invert the right subtree, and put them in swapped positions. Every node is processed exactly once, so the time is O(n). The recursion depth equals the height of the tree, which is O(n) in the worst case for a skewed tree and O(log n) for a balanced one; an explicit stack or queue removes the risk of stack overflow. To return the answer in the input format, run a level-order traversal and write null for missing children, then trim the trailing nulls.
followups: How would you do it iteratively with a stack or queue?
Does the order of swapping and recursing matter?

title: Balanced Binary Tree
statement: A binary tree is height-balanced if, for every node, the heights of its left and right subtrees differ by at most 1. Given a tree as a level-order array with null for missing children, return true if it is height-balanced. The tree has 0 to 5000 nodes.
hint: Compute heights bottom-up and report a failure as soon as you see a node whose subtrees differ by more than 1.
approach: The naive way computes the height of both subtrees for every node, which repeats work and costs O(n^2) on a skewed tree. A single bottom-up pass is better: write a function that returns the height of a subtree, or a special value (for example -1) if the subtree is already unbalanced. For a node, get the height of the left and right subtrees; if either is -1 pass -1 upward; if their difference is more than 1, return -1; otherwise return 1 + max(left, right). The tree is balanced when the root does not return -1. Each node is visited once, so the total time is O(n), and the recursion stack uses O(h) memory. An empty tree has height 0 and is balanced.
followups: Why is the top-down approach O(n^2) in the worst case?
How do AVL trees keep the balance condition?

title: Subtree of Another Tree
statement: Given two binary trees root and subRoot (each as a level-order array with null for missing children), return true if root contains a node whose whole subtree (the node and all its descendants) has exactly the same structure and values as subRoot. root has up to 2000 nodes, subRoot up to 1000.
hint: For each node of root, ask "is the tree starting here identical to subRoot?"
approach: Split the problem into two small recursive checks. First, sameTree(a, b): both empty is true, one empty is false, otherwise values must be equal and both pairs of children must be the same. Second, isSubtree: walk over every node of root, and at each node run sameTree against subRoot; if any run succeeds return true. Note that a match must include every descendant: the node with the equal value is not enough, as the tree below it may have extra nodes. In the worst case sameTree runs for each node of root and costs the size of subRoot, giving O(n * m). A linear alternative serialises both trees with explicit null markers and tests a substring match.
followups: How would you do this in O(n + m) with tree serialisation and KMP?
How would Merkle-style hashing of subtrees help?

title: Count Good Nodes in Binary Tree
statement: In a binary tree, a node X is good if no node on the path from the root to X has a value greater than X (the root is always good). Given the tree as a level-order array with null for missing children, return the number of good nodes. The tree has 1 to 100000 nodes, values between -10000 and 10000.
hint: Pass the maximum value seen on the path so far down with the recursion.
approach: Whether a node is good depends only on the maximum value on the path from the root to it. Do a depth-first traversal that carries this running maximum as an argument. At a node, if its value is at least the maximum so far, count it and update the maximum to its value. Then recurse into both children with the updated maximum. Every node is visited once with O(1) work, so the time is O(n). Starting the maximum at negative infinity makes the root good automatically. The recursion depth equals the tree height; for very skewed trees an explicit stack of (node, maxSoFar) pairs avoids stack overflow. The total count is the sum of the counts from the two sides plus one if the current node is good.
followups: How would you count nodes that are greater than every ancestor strictly?
How would you also return the list of good nodes?

title: Construct Binary Tree from Preorder and Inorder Traversal
statement: You get the preorder and the inorder traversal of a binary tree whose values are all distinct. Rebuild the tree and return it as a level-order array, where null marks a missing child and trailing nulls are left out (for example [3,9,20,null,null,15,7]). Both arrays have the same length n, with 0 <= n <= 3000.
hint: The first value in preorder is always the root. Where does that value sit in the inorder array, and what does that tell you about the left and right subtrees?
approach: Preorder visits root, then left subtree, then right subtree, so the next unused preorder value is always the root of the subtree we are building. Inorder visits left, root, right, so the position of that root in inorder splits the values into a left part and a right part. We build recursively over an inorder range: take the next preorder value, find its inorder index with a hash map (so lookup is O(1) instead of scanning), build the left range, then the right range. Because preorder is consumed left to right and the left subtree comes before the right subtree, one shared pointer into preorder is enough.
followups: What if the tree is given by inorder and postorder instead?
Why do preorder and postorder alone not identify a tree uniquely?
Can you avoid recursion depth problems on a very skewed tree?

title: Serialize and Deserialize Binary Tree
statement: Design a way to turn a binary tree into a string and back, so that no information is lost. The function roundTrip(tree) receives the tree as a level-order array (null for missing children, no trailing nulls), builds the tree, calls your serialize to get a string, calls your deserialize on that string, and returns the rebuilt tree as a level-order array. A correct codec returns exactly the input. Node values are integers in [-1000, 1000], and the tree has up to 10^4 nodes.
hint: A preorder walk is ambiguous unless you also record where the empty children are. What marker can you write for a missing child?
approach: Walk the tree in preorder and write each value, writing a marker such as # for every missing child. With the markers, the string describes the full shape: reading it left to right, a value means "make a node, then read its left subtree, then its right subtree", and a # means "this subtree is empty". Deserialize splits the string by commas and consumes tokens with one shared index in the same recursive order. Every node and every null is written once, so the work is linear. Using a delimiter between tokens keeps multi-digit and negative numbers unambiguous.
followups: Can you do it with a level-order (BFS) format instead, like LeetCode shows it?
If the tree is a BST, how can you drop the null markers and still rebuild it?
How would you make the string shorter for a large, nearly full tree?

title: Convert Sorted Array to Binary Search Tree
statement: Given an array of distinct integers sorted in increasing order, build a height-balanced binary search tree (the two subtrees of every node differ in height by at most 1) and return it as a level-order array with null for missing children and no trailing nulls. Many balanced trees exist, so to make the answer unique use this rule: for a range of indexes lo..hi, the root is the element at index floor((lo+hi)/2) (the lower middle). The array has 0 to 10^4 elements.
hint: If you pick the middle element as the root, what do the left half and the right half of the array become?
approach: In a sorted array the middle element is a natural root: everything to its left is smaller and everything to its right is larger, which is exactly the BST rule. Choosing the middle also splits the remaining elements into two halves whose sizes differ by at most one, and recursing on each half gives subtrees whose heights differ by at most one, so the whole tree stays balanced. We recurse on index ranges instead of slicing the array, so no copies are made. Each element becomes a node exactly once. Recursion depth is about log n, so the stack is never a problem.
complexity: O(n) time, O(log n) extra space (recursion)
followups: How would you do the same for a sorted singly linked list without random access?
What changes if the tree must be balanced but the input is unsorted?
How do you prove the height of the result is floor(log2 n) + 1?

title: Flatten Binary Tree to Linked List
statement: A binary tree is given as a level-order array (null for missing children). Rearrange its nodes in place so that every left pointer becomes empty and the right pointers form a chain that visits the nodes in preorder order (root, left subtree, right subtree). Your function must do this on the node objects and then return the list of values you meet when you follow right pointers from the root. The tree has up to 2000 nodes.
hint: For a node with a left child, where should the old right subtree end up? Think about the last node of the left subtree.
approach: In preorder, the whole left subtree comes right after the node and before the right subtree. So for a node with a left child, find the rightmost node of the left subtree (it is the last node in preorder of that subtree), attach the node's old right subtree to it, then move the left subtree into the right pointer and set left to null. Then step to the right child and repeat. Every node is processed once, and each rightmost walk is only repeated along a path that is later rewired, so total work stays linear and we need no stack or recursion.
followups: Can you do it with a recursive post-order style approach (right, left, previous)?
How would you flatten into inorder order instead?
What is the space cost of the recursive version on a skewed tree?

title: Insert into a Binary Search Tree
statement: A binary search tree is given as a level-order array (null for missing children), together with a value val that is not in the tree. Insert val as a new leaf, going down from the root like a normal BST search, and return the new tree as a level-order array with no trailing nulls. Do not rebalance or restructure existing nodes. The tree has up to 10^4 nodes, and an empty tree is allowed.
hint: Search for val as if it were there. Where does the search stop?
approach: A BST search for a missing value ends at an empty child slot, and that slot is the only place the value can go without breaking the ordering. So walk down from the root: go left if val is smaller than the current node, right otherwise. When the chosen child is empty, put the new node there and stop. Nothing else changes, so every other node keeps its place and the BST property stays true. If the tree is empty, the new node becomes the root. The loop version uses constant extra space; the recursive version is the same idea.
complexity: O(h) time, O(1) space (h = tree height)
followups: How would you keep the tree balanced after the insert (AVL or red-black)?
What if duplicates are allowed? Where should they go?
Can you write it recursively and return the new subtree root?

title: Kth Smallest Element in a BST
statement: A binary search tree is given as a level-order array (null for missing children) with distinct integer values, plus an integer k (1-indexed). Return the k-th smallest value in the tree. The tree has n nodes with 1 <= k <= n <= 10^4.
hint: What order does an inorder walk visit the values of a BST in?
approach: An inorder traversal of a BST visits the values in increasing order, so the k-th node visited is the answer. We do the traversal with an explicit stack: push all the way down the left side, then pop a node, count it, and move to its right child. We stop as soon as the counter reaches k, so we never visit the rest of the tree. This costs O(h + k) time, which is much less than n when k is small. The explicit stack also avoids deep recursion on skewed trees.
followups: If the tree is modified often and k-th queries are frequent, what would you store in each node?
How would you find the k-th largest instead?
Can you do it in O(1) extra space with Morris traversal?

title: Lowest Common Ancestor of a Binary Search Tree
statement: A binary search tree with distinct values is given as a level-order array (null for missing children). p and q are two different values that both exist in the tree. Return the value of their lowest common ancestor: the deepest node that has both p and q in its subtree (a node counts as being in its own subtree). The tree has 2 to 10^5 nodes.
hint: Compare p and q with the current node. When do they stop going to the same side?
approach: Start at the root. If both p and q are smaller than the current value, the LCA must be in the left subtree, so go left. If both are larger, go right. Otherwise p and q are on different sides of the current node, or one of them equals it, and that means the current node is the deepest node that still covers both: it is the LCA. This uses the BST ordering to skip entire subtrees, so we follow one path from the root and never need parent pointers or a full search.
followups: How does the answer change for a general binary tree that is not a BST?
What if p or q might not be in the tree?
Can you find it if you only have parent pointers?

title: Delete Node in a BST
statement: A binary search tree with distinct values is given as a level-order array (null for missing children), plus a value key. If the key is in the tree, delete that node; otherwise leave the tree unchanged. Return the resulting tree as a level-order array with no trailing nulls. To make the answer unique, use this rule: a node with no child is removed, a node with one child is replaced by that child, and a node with two children takes the value of the smallest node in its right subtree (its inorder successor), which is then removed from the right subtree. The tree has up to 10^4 nodes.
hint: Handle the cases by number of children. The two-children case needs a replacement value that keeps the ordering valid.
approach: First search for the key like in any BST, recursing left or right and re-attaching the returned subtree. When we reach the node: with no left child we return the right child, with no right child we return the left child (this covers leaf nodes too). With two children we cannot simply drop the node, so we copy in the value of its inorder successor, the minimum of the right subtree. That value is larger than everything on the left and smaller than everything else on the right, so the order stays valid. Then we delete the successor from the right subtree, which has at most one child, so it falls into the easy case.
followups: What changes if you use the inorder predecessor instead of the successor?
How would you avoid copying values and relink the nodes instead?
How do deletions make a plain BST unbalanced, and how do AVL trees fix it?

title: Subsets II
statement: Given an integer array nums that may contain duplicates, return all distinct subsets (the power set without repeated subsets). Each subset lists its numbers in non-decreasing order, and the subsets can be returned in any order. The array has 1 to 10 elements, each between -10 and 10.
hint: Sort first. When you loop over choices at one depth, what should you do when the next number equals the one you just tried?
approach: Sort the array so equal numbers sit next to each other. Build subsets with the usual recursion: at each call, record the current path as a subset, then try adding each later number one at a time and recurse. To avoid duplicates, inside one loop we skip a number if it equals the previous number in the same loop (and is not the first choice of that loop). Choosing the same value twice at the same depth would create the same subset again, but choosing it at a deeper level is still allowed, so subsets with repeated values such as [2,2] are produced exactly once.
followups: How would you count the distinct subsets without generating them?
Can you do it iteratively by only extending the subsets added in the last round when a value repeats?
What if the answer must be in lexicographic order?

title: Permutations II
statement: Given an array of integers nums that may contain duplicates, return all distinct permutations. To make answers easy to compare, return them in lexicographic order (sort nums first; at each position try the smallest unused value first). The array has 1 to 8 elements, each between -10 and 10.
hint: Sort the array. If two equal numbers are both unused, in what order must they be placed so you never create the same permutation twice?
approach: Sort nums and build permutations position by position with a used[] array. The duplicate trouble comes from equal numbers being swapped with each other, which gives the same sequence. We fix this by forcing equal numbers to be used in their sorted order: skip index i if nums[i] equals nums[i-1] and index i-1 is still unused. That means a copy of a value can only be placed after the earlier copy has already been placed on the current path. Every distinct permutation is then built exactly one way, and because we always try smaller values first, the results come out in lexicographic order.
complexity: O(n * n!) time, O(n) extra space
followups: Can you solve it by counting each value instead of using a used[] array?
How would you return only the k-th permutation without generating the others?
How would you compute the next lexicographic permutation in place?

title: Combination Sum II
statement: Given an array of positive integers candidates (which may repeat) and a positive integer target, return all distinct combinations of candidates that add up to target. Each element of the array can be used at most once, and no two returned combinations may be the same list of values. Each combination is listed in non-decreasing order; the combinations can be returned in any order. The array has up to 100 elements, each from 1 to 50, and target is at most 30.
hint: Sort the array. This lets you stop early when a number is too big, and skip repeated values at the same depth.
approach: Sort candidates, then do a depth-first search over the start index, keeping a running remaining target. At each step try each candidate from the start index onward and recurse with the next index (so each element is used at most once). Two prunings make it fast and correct. If the candidate is bigger than the remaining target, we can break the loop, because all later candidates are even bigger. If the candidate equals the previous one in the same loop, we skip it, since starting with the same value again would repeat a combination that was already explored. When the remaining target reaches 0 we save the path.
complexity: O(2^n) time in the worst case, O(n) space
followups: What changes if every element may be used any number of times (Combination Sum)?
How would you count the combinations instead of listing them?
Why does sorting help both with duplicates and with pruning?

title: Restore IP Addresses
statement: Given a string s made only of digits, return every valid IPv4 address that can be formed by inserting three dots into s (without reordering or removing digits). A valid address has four parts, each a number from 0 to 255 written without leading zeros (the part "0" is fine, "01" is not). Return the addresses as strings such as "255.255.11.135", in any order. The string length is 1 to 20.
hint: Choose the length of each of the four parts (1 to 3 digits). Which parts are valid, and how can you stop early when the leftover digits cannot fit?
approach: We cut the string into exactly four parts using recursion over the position and the number of parts built so far. For each part we try lengths 1, 2 and 3 and keep the piece only if it is a valid number: no leading zero unless the piece is exactly "0", and its value is at most 255. We also prune with simple length math: the remaining digits must be between one and three per remaining part, otherwise we return immediately. When we have four parts and have used every digit, we join the parts with dots and save the result. The search tree has at most 3^4 leaves, so it is tiny.
complexity: O(1) time (at most 81 leaves), O(1) extra space
followups: How would you generalize to IPv6 or to any number of parts?
How would you only count the valid addresses, using DP?
How many valid addresses can a string of length 12 have at most?

title: Sliding Puzzle
statement: A board has 2 rows and 3 columns holding the numbers 0 to 5 once each; 0 is the empty square. In one move you swap 0 with a square that touches it left, right, up or down. The goal state is [[1,2,3],[4,5,0]]. Given the starting board, return the least number of moves needed to reach the goal, or -1 if it is impossible.
hint: Think of every arrangement of the board as a node in a graph. There are only 6! = 720 nodes.
approach: Each arrangement of the board is a state, and one move connects two states, so the question is a shortest path in an unweighted graph, which BFS solves. We write the board as a 6-character string and keep, for every position of 0, the list of positions it can swap with. BFS starts from the given state, and for each state it swaps the 0 with every allowed neighbor to get new states. A visited set makes sure each state is expanded once. The first time we pop the goal string, the depth is the minimum number of moves. If the queue empties first, the goal is unreachable (half of the arrangements are).
followups: How would you handle a 3x3 puzzle where there are 362,880 states?
How can A* with the Manhattan distance speed this up?
How can you tell from the permutation parity whether a board is solvable?

title: Minimum Knight Moves
statement: A chess knight stands on (0, 0) of an infinite board. A move jumps 2 squares in one direction and 1 square at a right angle (8 possible jumps). Given a target square (x, y), return the minimum number of knight moves to reach it. It is always reachable. Limits: -300 <= x, y <= 300.
hint: The board is symmetric. Can you work only with |x| and |y|, and keep the search area small?
approach: The board is an implicit unweighted graph, so BFS from (0,0) finds the shortest number of moves. The board is symmetric under reflections, so we only need the case x >= 0 and y >= 0: replace the target by (|x|, |y|). A path to such a target may still need to step slightly outside the positive quadrant, so we allow coordinates down to -2 and ignore squares beyond that, which keeps the search area small instead of infinite. A set remembers visited squares. We expand level by level and return the level number when we pop the target.
complexity: O(x * y) time, O(x * y) space
followups: Why is a lower bound of -2 enough for the search area?
Can you speed it up with bidirectional BFS?
Is there a closed-form formula for most targets?

title: Walls and Gates
statement: A grid rooms has cells with three kinds of values: -1 is a wall, 0 is a gate, and 2147483647 (call it INF) is an empty room. Fill every empty room with the number of steps to its nearest gate, moving up, down, left or right through non-wall cells. Rooms that cannot reach any gate stay INF. Return the filled grid. The grid has up to 250 x 250 cells.
hint: Do not search from every room. Start from all the gates at the same time.
approach: Running a BFS from each empty room is far too slow. Instead we reverse the question: start one BFS from all gates together (a multi-source BFS). Put every gate in the queue with distance 0, then expand level by level. When we reach an empty room (value INF) for the first time, we write the current distance into it and add it to the queue. Because BFS processes cells in order of increasing distance, the first visit is the shortest, and the value being no longer INF also serves as the visited marker. Rooms not reachable from any gate are never touched, so they keep INF.
complexity: O(m * n) time, O(m * n) space
followups: What changes if diagonal moves are allowed?
What if cells have different costs to enter? (Dijkstra instead of BFS)
How would you answer the question for the farthest room from any gate?

title: Snakes and Ladders
statement: You are given an n x n board whose cells are numbered 1 to n*n in a zig-zag order: start at the bottom-left cell as 1, go right along the bottom row, then go left along the next row up, and so on. A cell value of -1 means a normal square; any other value is the number of the square a snake or ladder sends you to. You start on square 1. In each move you roll any number from 1 to 6 and go to the square that many ahead (if it exists); if that square has a snake or ladder, you must take it (only once per move, no chaining). Return the minimum number of moves to reach square n*n, or -1 if impossible. 2 <= n <= 20.
hint: Turn square numbers into board coordinates carefully, then it is a BFS where each square has up to 6 neighbors.
approach: Each square is a node and a dice roll is an edge, so the minimum number of moves is a BFS distance from square 1 to square n*n. The only tricky part is converting a square number s to a row and column in the zig-zag layout: row from the bottom is (s-1) / n, and the column runs left to right on even rows from the bottom and right to left on odd ones. For each square we try the destinations s+1 to s+6 (capped at n*n), apply the snake or ladder jump if the cell is not -1, and push the result if it has not been visited. We take at most one jump per move, as required. The first time we reach n*n, the level number is the answer.
followups: What changes if you may choose whether to take a ladder?
How would you also return the sequence of squares used?
Why does BFS on squares give a correct answer even with snakes that go backwards?

title: Minimum Height Trees
statement: A tree has n nodes labelled 0 to n-1, given as a list of n-1 undirected edges. If you pick any node as the root, the tree gets a height (the longest path from the root down). Return the labels of all nodes that give the smallest possible height. There are one or two such nodes. 1 <= n <= 2*10^4.
hint: The best roots are in the middle of the longest path. How can you walk inward from the leaves?
approach: The roots that minimise the height are the centers of the tree, and a tree has one or two centers. We find them by peeling leaves, which works like a topological sort on degrees. Compute the degree of each node and put all leaves (degree 1) in a queue. Remove all current leaves at once, lower the degree of their neighbors, and the neighbors that become leaves form the next layer. Repeat while more than two nodes remain. The last one or two nodes left are the centers. Peeling layer by layer is important: removing one leaf at a time would not keep the nodes balanced.
followups: How would you find the centers using two BFS runs (the tree diameter)?
Why can a tree never have three centers?
How would you compute the height for every possible root in O(n)?

title: Parallel Courses
statement: There are n courses numbered 1 to n. Each relation [a, b] means course a must be finished before course b can start. In one semester you can take any number of courses, as long as all their prerequisites were finished in earlier semesters. Return the minimum number of semesters needed to finish all courses, or -1 if it is impossible because of a cycle. 1 <= n <= 5000.
hint: Take every course whose prerequisites are done, all in the same semester. How many rounds does that need?
approach: This is a topological sort where we count layers. Build the graph and the in-degree of every course. All courses with in-degree 0 can be taken in semester one, so we put them in a queue. We then process the queue one layer at a time: all courses in the current layer are one semester, and finishing them reduces the in-degree of their followers. Followers that reach 0 form the next layer. The number of layers is the number of semesters, which equals the longest chain of prerequisites. If the number of courses we processed is smaller than n, some courses were stuck in a cycle, so we return -1.
complexity: O(n + E) time, O(n + E) space
followups: What if at most k courses can be taken per semester (Parallel Courses II)?
How would you solve it with DFS and memoization of the longest path?
How would you list which courses are in which semester?

title: Find All Possible Recipes from Given Supplies
statement: You have recipes (names) and, for each recipe i, a list ingredients[i] of things it needs. An ingredient can be a raw supply or another recipe. supplies lists the raw items you have in unlimited amount. A recipe can be made if all its ingredients are available, either as supplies or as recipes you can already make. Return the names of all recipes you can make, in any order. Up to 100 recipes; names are lowercase strings, all distinct.
hint: Think of ingredients as prerequisites of a recipe. Start from the supplies and unlock recipes as their needs are met.
approach: Treat every recipe as a node whose in-degree is the number of ingredients it needs. Each ingredient points to the recipes that use it. We start a queue with all supplies; when we pop an item, we lower the counter of every recipe that needs it. If a counter reaches 0, that recipe can now be cooked, so we add it to the answer and to the queue because it may itself be an ingredient of other recipes. Recipes that depend on something never available, or that are in a dependency cycle, never reach 0 and are not returned. Each ingredient link is handled once, so it is linear in the input size.
complexity: O(R + I) time and space (R recipes, I total ingredient entries)
followups: How would you also return an order in which to cook them?
What if each supply only comes in a limited amount?
How would you solve it with DFS and cycle detection instead?

title: Sequence Reconstruction
statement: nums is a permutation of the integers 1 to n. sequences is a list of sequences, each a subsequence of some unknown ordering. Decide whether nums is the only shortest sequence that has every sequence in sequences as a subsequence. Return true if nums is the unique answer, otherwise false. 1 <= n <= 10^4, and every number in sequences is between 1 and n.
hint: Each pair of neighbors in a sequence gives an order rule. When is a topological order unique?
approach: Every pair of consecutive numbers in a sequence is a rule "a comes before b", so we build a directed graph from them. nums is the only valid ordering exactly when the graph has a unique topological order. In Kahn's algorithm, the order is unique if and only if the queue holds exactly one node at every step: two nodes in the queue would mean either could come first. So we run Kahn's algorithm, check that the queue size is 1 each time, and check that the node we pop equals the next number of nums. If we process all n numbers this way, the answer is true. A cycle or a conflicting order makes the queue stall or mismatch, giving false.
complexity: O(n + total length of sequences) time and space
followups: How would you count the number of valid orderings if it is not unique?
Why is checking only consecutive pairs enough?
How would the answer change if sequences could use numbers outside nums?

title: Path with Maximum Probability
statement: An undirected graph has n nodes (0 to n-1). Edge i connects edges[i] = [a, b] and a signal crosses it successfully with probability succProb[i] (between 0 and 1). The probability of a path is the product of its edge probabilities. Return the maximum probability of getting from start to end, or 0 if there is no path. Answers are compared exactly, so the tests only multiply probabilities that are exact in binary (like 0.5 and 0.25) or use a single edge. n is up to 10^4.
hint: This is Dijkstra, but you multiply instead of add, and you want the largest value instead of the smallest.
approach: Dijkstra works whenever extending a path can never improve it. Here every edge probability is at most 1, so multiplying can only keep or lower the probability, which is the same property as non-negative weights. We keep best[v], the best known probability to reach v, with best[start] = 1. A max-heap pops the node with the highest probability. For each edge we compute p * edgeProb and, if it beats best of the neighbor, update it and push. The first time the end node is popped, its value is final. If the heap runs out, end is unreachable and the answer is 0. Taking logarithms would turn this into a normal shortest path.
complexity: O((n + E) log n) time, O(n + E) space
followups: Why does Dijkstra still work when we maximise a product of numbers in [0, 1]?
Can Bellman-Ford solve it, and when would you prefer that?
How would you avoid floating-point underflow on very long paths?

title: Swim in Rising Water
statement: An n x n grid holds each integer from 0 to n*n-1 exactly once; grid[r][c] is the height of that cell. Water rises over time: at time t you may stand on any cell with height <= t, and you can swim from a cell to a neighboring cell (up, down, left, right) if both have height <= t. You start at the top-left cell at time 0. Return the least time t at which you can reach the bottom-right cell. 1 <= n <= 50.
hint: The cost of a path is the highest cell on it. This is a shortest path where "length" means the maximum, not the sum.
approach: For a given path the time you need is the largest height on it, and we want the path with the smallest such maximum. This is a bottleneck shortest-path problem that Dijkstra solves if we replace the sum by max. Keep a min-heap of (time, cell), where time is the best known maximum height to reach that cell. Start with the top-left cell at its own height. Pop the cell with the smallest time, and for each unvisited neighbor push (max(time, neighbor height), neighbor). When we pop the bottom-right cell, its time is the answer. Max is monotonic (never decreases along a path), so the first pop of a cell is already optimal.
complexity: O(n^2 log n) time, O(n^2) space
followups: Can you solve it with binary search on the time plus a BFS?
Can union-find solve it by adding cells in increasing height order?
What changes if heights are not distinct?

title: Minimum Cost to Make at Least One Valid Path in a Grid
statement: Every cell of an m x n grid holds an arrow: 1 means go right, 2 left, 3 down, 4 up. Starting at the top-left cell you follow the arrow of the cell you are on to move to its neighbor (you may not leave the grid). You can change the arrow of any cell at most once, and each change costs 1. Return the minimum total cost so that a path of arrows exists from the top-left cell to the bottom-right cell. 1 <= m, n <= 100.
hint: Moving along the arrow is free, moving any other way costs 1. What kind of shortest path has only 0 and 1 weights?
approach: Make a graph where each cell has an edge to each of its four neighbors. The edge that follows the cell's own arrow costs 0, and the other three cost 1 (changing the arrow). Now the answer is the shortest path from the top-left to the bottom-right cell. With only 0 and 1 weights we can use 0-1 BFS: keep a deque, push the endpoint of a 0-weight edge to the front and the endpoint of a 1-weight edge to the back. The deque then stays ordered by distance, so each cell's first pop is final. This is like Dijkstra without a heap. We relax a neighbor only if we found a strictly smaller distance.
complexity: O(m * n) time, O(m * n) space
followups: Why is 0-1 BFS correct and not just a plain BFS?
How would you solve it with Dijkstra and what does it cost extra?
How would you recover the cells whose arrows were changed?

title: Min Cost to Connect All Points
statement: You are given n points on a 2D plane as [x, y] pairs. The cost of joining two points is their Manhattan distance |x1 - x2| + |y1 - y2|. Return the minimum total cost to connect all points so that there is exactly one simple path between any two points (a minimum spanning tree). 1 <= n <= 1000 and coordinates are within 10^6 in absolute value.
hint: Every pair of points is a possible edge. Grow a tree from one point, always adding the cheapest edge to a point not yet in the tree.
approach: The graph is complete, with n(n-1)/2 edges, so a dense-graph method is best: Prim's algorithm with an array instead of a heap. Keep minDist[i], the cheapest edge from the current tree to point i, starting with point 0 in the tree. Repeat n-1 times: pick the point not in the tree with the smallest minDist, add its cost to the total, mark it in the tree, then update minDist for all other points using the distance from the newly added point. Prim works because the cheapest edge leaving any cut is always part of some minimum spanning tree (the cut property). The result is O(n^2), which beats sorting all edges for Kruskal.
followups: When would Kruskal with a union-find be better than Prim?
How could you reduce the number of candidate edges for Euclidean distance?
How would you add a point and update the tree cheaply?

title: Connecting Cities With Minimum Cost
statement: There are n cities labelled 1 to n. connections is a list of [cityA, cityB, cost]: you can build a road between those two cities for that cost. Return the minimum total cost to build roads so that every city can reach every other city, or -1 if that is impossible. 1 <= n <= 10^4.
hint: Sort the roads by cost and take a road only if it joins two groups of cities that are not connected yet.
approach: We need a minimum spanning tree, and Kruskal's algorithm is the simplest way. Sort all connections by cost. Go through them from cheapest to most expensive and use a union-find structure to check whether the two cities are already connected. If not, we build the road: add its cost and merge the groups. A road between cities that are already connected would only create a cycle, so we skip it. This greedy choice is safe by the cut property: the cheapest edge that joins two different components is in some minimum spanning tree. After the pass, if all n cities are in one group (n-1 roads were built), return the total, otherwise -1.
complexity: O(E log E) time, O(n) space
followups: How would Prim's algorithm compare here?
What if some roads already exist for free?
How do you find the second-best spanning tree?

title: Optimize Water Distribution in a Village
statement: A village has n houses numbered 1 to n. Each house can get water in two ways: by building its own well, which costs wells[i-1] for house i, or by being linked with a pipe to another house that has water. pipes is a list of [house1, house2, cost] pipe options (the pipe works both ways). Return the minimum total cost so that every house has water. n is up to 10^4.
hint: Add an imaginary source node. What does a well look like if it is an edge from that node?
approach: Add a virtual node 0 that stands for the water source. Building a well in house i is the same as a pipe between node 0 and house i with cost wells[i-1]. Now the problem is: connect all n+1 nodes as cheaply as possible, which is a minimum spanning tree. We put the real pipes and the well edges together, sort by cost, and run Kruskal with union-find: take an edge if it joins two different groups. Houses connected through a chain of pipes to one well share that well; houses with a cheaper well than any pipe get their own. The sum of the chosen edge costs is the answer. A spanning tree always exists because every house has a well edge.
complexity: O((n + P) log(n + P)) time, O(n + P) space
followups: How would the answer change if a well could supply only a limited number of houses?
Can you explain why adding a virtual node preserves optimality?
How would you handle pipes that already exist and cost nothing?

title: Find Critical and Pseudo-Critical Edges in Minimum Spanning Tree
statement: A connected, weighted, undirected graph has n nodes (0 to n-1) and edges[i] = [a, b, weight]. A minimum spanning tree (MST) is a cheapest set of edges connecting all nodes. An edge is critical if removing it from the graph makes the MST cost go up (it is in every MST). An edge is pseudo-critical if it is in some MST but not in all of them. Return [critical, pseudo], two lists of edge indexes, each in increasing order. 2 <= n <= 100, up to 200 edges.
hint: Compute the base MST cost. Then test each edge twice: once forbidding it, once forcing it in.
approach: First compute the cost of a normal MST with Kruskal. Then for every edge i, run Kruskal two more times. If we leave edge i out and the graph becomes disconnected or the cost rises above the base cost, edge i is in every MST, so it is critical. Otherwise, if we force edge i into the tree first (union its endpoints, add its weight) and then finish with Kruskal, and the total still equals the base cost, then edge i belongs to at least one MST. Since it was not critical, it is pseudo-critical. Edges that fail both tests are in no MST. With at most 200 edges, about 400 Kruskal runs are cheap.
complexity: O(E^2 * alpha(n)) time, O(E + n) space
followups: Can you find the critical edges in near-linear time using bridges in the graph of equal-weight edges?
Why does forcing an edge and still matching the base cost prove it is in some MST?
How would you count the number of distinct MSTs?

title: Accounts Merge
statement: accounts[i] is a list: the first item is a person's name and the rest are email addresses of that account. Two accounts belong to the same person if they share at least one email (different people can have the same name, but never share an email). Merge accounts of the same person and return them as lists [name, email1, email2, ...] with the emails sorted in ascending order (plain string comparison). Order the merged accounts by their first (smallest) email. Up to 1000 accounts, each with up to 10 emails.
hint: Treat each account as a node and connect two accounts when they share an email. A map from email to the first account that used it helps.
