approach: Use union-find over account indexes. Walk through the accounts and keep a map from each email to the index of the account where we first saw it. When an email was already seen in another account, union the two accounts, because they must belong to the same person. After all unions, group the emails by the root of their account, sort the emails in each group, and put the name in front (every account in a group has the same name). Finally sort the groups by their smallest email so the output order is fixed. The unions are almost constant time with path compression, so the sorting of emails dominates the cost.
complexity: O(N log N) time where N is the total number of emails, O(N) space
followups: How would you solve it with DFS over an email graph instead?
What if account names for the same person can differ?
How would you handle a stream of new accounts arriving one by one?

title: Most Stones Removed with Same Row or Column
statement: Stones sit on distinct integer points of a 2D plane, given as stones[i] = [row, col]. In one move you may remove a stone if some other stone that is still on the plane shares its row or its column. Return the largest number of stones that can be removed. 1 <= stones.length <= 1000 and coordinates are between 0 and 10^4.
hint: Stones that share a row or column form a group. How many stones of a group can you remove, and which one must stay?
approach: Put two stones in the same group if they share a row or column, directly or through a chain of other stones. Inside one connected group, we can always remove every stone except one: remove stones in an order that peels the group like a tree from the leaves, so each removed stone still has a neighbor in its row or column. The last stone stays because it has no partner. So the answer is the number of stones minus the number of groups. To find the groups, treat each row and each column as a node (columns shifted by 10001), and union row r with column c for every stone. The number of components that contain stones is the number of groups.
followups: Why is it always possible to leave exactly one stone per group?
Can you solve it with DFS over stones instead of union-find?
How would you count the ways to choose which stone remains in each group?

title: Graph Valid Tree
statement: There are n nodes labelled 0 to n-1 and a list of undirected edges. Decide whether these edges form a valid tree: all nodes are connected, and there are no cycles. Return true or false. 1 <= n <= 2000, and there are no repeated edges.
hint: A tree on n nodes has exactly n-1 edges. What else must hold?
approach: A graph is a tree exactly when it is connected and has no cycle, which is the same as being connected with exactly n-1 edges. So first check that the number of edges is n-1; if not, the answer is false (too few edges cannot connect everything, too many must contain a cycle). Then use union-find: for each edge, try to union its endpoints. If the endpoints are already in the same set, this edge closes a cycle, so return false. With n-1 successful unions on n nodes there is a single component, so the graph is connected and acyclic. The same check can be done with a DFS that tracks the parent node.
followups: How would you check it with a DFS or BFS and a visited set?
What if the edges arrive one at a time and you must report the first edge that breaks the tree?
How does the answer change for a directed graph (a rooted tree)?

title: Number of Islands II
statement: An m x n grid starts as all water. positions is a list of [row, col] cells; at step i that cell turns into land. After each step, report the number of islands, where an island is a group of land cells connected up, down, left or right. Return the array of counts, one per step. A position may appear more than once (turning land into land changes nothing). 1 <= m, n <= 10^4, up to 10^4 positions.
hint: You only add land, never remove it. A structure that merges groups is a good fit.
approach: Union-find handles additions well. Number cells as r * n + c and keep the count of islands. When a cell turns into land for the first time, count one more island, mark it as land, and look at its four neighbors. For every neighbor that is already land, try to union the two cells; each union that really joins two different islands lowers the count by one. If the cell was already land we just record the current count again. After each step, push the count to the result. Doing a fresh flood fill after every addition would be far slower, since each step could scan the entire grid.
complexity: O(k * alpha(m * n)) time, O(k) space for k positions
followups: How would you also support removing land (turning land back to water)?
How can you keep memory small when the grid is huge but positions are few?
What is the benefit of union by size or rank here?

title: Search Suggestions System
statement: products is a list of lowercase strings and searchWord is a lowercase string being typed one character at a time. After each typed character, suggest at most three products that start with the text typed so far. If more than three match, suggest the three that come first in alphabetical order. Return a list with one list of suggestions per typed character. Up to 1000 products and a search word of up to 1000 characters.
hint: Sort the products. Products with the same prefix are then next to each other, and the first three come first.
approach: Sort the products alphabetically, then insert them into a trie in that order. In every trie node keep a short list of suggestions: when a product passes through a node and the node holds fewer than three, add the product. Since products arrive in sorted order, the three kept are always the three smallest with that prefix. To answer, walk down the trie with the characters of searchWord; at each step collect the node's list. If a character is missing from the trie, all later answers are empty lists. This moves the work to the build step and makes each answer a plain lookup.
complexity: O(total characters + sort) time, O(total characters) space
followups: How would you do it without a trie, using binary search on the sorted list?
How would you rank suggestions by popularity instead of alphabetically?
How would you support the products list changing over time?

title: Replace Words
statement: dictionary is a list of "root" words, and sentence is a string of lowercase words separated by single spaces. Replace every word of the sentence that has a root as a prefix with that root; if several roots fit, use the shortest one. Words with no matching root stay as they are. Return the new sentence. Up to 1000 roots, and the sentence has up to 10^6 characters.
hint: For each word, walk down a prefix tree of the roots and stop at the first place where a root ends.
approach: Insert all roots into a trie and mark the nodes where a root ends. For each word of the sentence, walk down the trie one letter at a time, building the prefix as we go. The first time we reach a node marked as the end of a root, that prefix is the shortest root that matches, so we use it as the replacement. If we fall off the trie or reach the end of the word first, the word has no root and we keep it unchanged. Stopping at the first marked node is what gives the shortest root. Each word costs at most its own length, so the whole sentence is linear.
complexity: O(total length of roots + sentence length) time and space

args: the cattle was rattled by the battery
tests.expected: the cat was rat by the bat

followups: How would you do it with a hash set of roots and checking each prefix length?
What if the replacement should be the longest matching root?
How would you handle punctuation and capital letters?

title: Map Sum Pairs
statement: Implement MapSum with insert(key, val) and sum(prefix). insert stores the pair; if the key already exists, its value is replaced by the new one. sum(prefix) returns the total of the values of all keys that start with the prefix (0 if none). Input: a list of operation names and a list of argument lists. Return a list: null for the constructor and insert, the number for sum. Keys are lowercase words up to 50 letters, values are from 1 to 1000, and there are up to 50 calls.
hint: In a trie, every node on the path of a key can keep a running total of the values of all keys passing through it.
approach: Store a trie where each node keeps sum, the total value of all keys that pass through that node. To answer sum(prefix) we only walk down the prefix and return the sum of the last node, or 0 if the path breaks. The only subtle part is overwriting an existing key. We keep a hash map from key to its current value; on insert we compute delta = newValue - oldValue (the old value is 0 for a new key), and then add delta to the sum of every node along the key's path. This way the totals stay correct no matter how often a key is overwritten. Insert costs the key length, and so does sum.
complexity: O(L) time per call (L = word length), O(total characters) space
followups: How would you do it without keeping totals in the nodes, by walking the subtree at query time?
What changes if you also need a remove(key) operation?
How would you answer the sum for prefixes with values that can be negative?

title: Maximum XOR of Two Numbers in an Array
statement: Given an array of non-negative integers nums, return the largest value of nums[i] XOR nums[j] over all pairs i, j (they may be equal indexes, giving 0). The array has 1 to 2*10^5 elements, each less than 2^31.
hint: To maximise XOR, for each number you want a partner whose bits are the opposite, starting with the highest bit.
approach: Write every number as 31 bits and insert it into a binary trie, from the highest bit to the lowest. For a number x, we walk the trie and at each bit try to go to the child with the opposite bit, because a 1 in a higher position of the XOR is worth more than all lower bits together. If that child exists we take it and add that bit to the result; if not, we must follow the same bit. After 31 steps, the path is the number that gives the best XOR with x. The answer is the maximum over all x. Greedy per bit is correct because the bits are ordered by value, and the trie always lets us check which options exist.
complexity: O(31 * n) time, O(31 * n) space
followups: Can you do it with a hash set of prefixes, one bit at a time?
How would you answer many queries "max XOR of x with any number in the set"?
What changes when numbers can be negative?

title: Reorganize String
statement: Given a lowercase string s, rearrange its letters so that no two equal letters are next to each other. Return the rearranged string, or "" if it is impossible. Many answers can exist, so to make the result unique build it like this: at each position put the letter that has the most copies left among the letters different from the previous one, and break ties by choosing the alphabetically smaller letter. 1 <= s.length <= 500.
hint: The most frequent letter is the hardest to place. Which letter should go next, and which one must you not use right now?
approach: Count the letters and keep them in a max-heap ordered by remaining count (ties by smaller letter). Repeatedly pop the top letter, append it to the answer, and decrease its count. The letter we just used must not come next, so we hold it aside for one step and push it back into the heap only after the next letter was chosen. Always using the most frequent available letter keeps the large counts from piling up at the end. If at some point the heap is empty but a held letter still has copies left, nothing else can separate them, so the answer is "". This succeeds exactly when the most frequent letter appears at most ceil(n/2) times.
complexity: O(n log 26) time, O(1) extra space
followups: Can you do it without a heap by placing the most frequent letter at even indexes first?
How would you require that equal letters are at least k apart?
How would you prove that the condition "max count <= ceil(n/2)" is enough?

title: Last Stone Weight
statement: You have an array stones of positive weights. Each turn, take the two heaviest stones and smash them together. If they weigh the same, both are destroyed. Otherwise the lighter one is destroyed and the heavier one is left with weight equal to the difference. Repeat until at most one stone is left, and return its weight (0 if no stone is left). 1 <= stones.length <= 30, weights up to 1000.
hint: You need the two largest values again and again, and new values are added back. Which data structure gives the largest quickly?
approach: A max-heap always gives the heaviest stone in O(log n). Put all stones in the heap. While at least two stones remain, pop the two largest, y >= x, and if they differ, push y - x back. The simulation follows the rules exactly, and each round removes at least one stone, so there are fewer than n rounds. When the loop ends, the heap has either one stone, whose weight is the answer, or none, so the answer is 0. Sorting the array each round would also work for the small limits here, but costs O(n log n) per round instead of O(log n).
complexity: O(n log n) time, O(n) space
followups: What if the stones are in the range 1 to 1000 and n is huge? (counting array)
How would you handle a continuous stream of new stones?
How does this relate to Last Stone Weight II, where you choose the pairs?

title: IPO
statement: A company can finish at most k projects before its IPO. Project i needs capital[i] to start and yields a pure profit of profits[i] when done; the profit is added to your capital right away. You begin with capital w. Choose at most k different projects, one after another, to maximise the final capital, and return that number. Up to 10^5 projects, and all values are non-negative.
hint: At each step you want the most profitable project among the ones you can afford. How do you keep the affordable ones ready as your capital grows?
approach: Greedy works: each finished project only increases our capital, so at every step the best choice is the most profitable project we can currently afford. To do this quickly, sort the projects by the capital they need. Keep a max-heap of profits of all affordable projects. Before each of the k rounds, move every project with capital <= current w from the sorted list into the heap. Then pop the largest profit and add it to w. If the heap is empty, no project is affordable and we stop early. Picking a smaller profit now can never help later, because affordability only depends on how much capital we have, and bigger profit gives more capital.
complexity: O(n log n + k log n) time, O(n) space
followups: What if each project can also be done more than once?
What changes if completing a project costs capital that is returned later?
Why would choosing the project with the smallest capital requirement first be wrong?

title: Smallest Range Covering Elements from K Lists
statement: You are given k lists of integers, each sorted in non-decreasing order. Find the smallest range [lo, hi] that contains at least one number from every list. A range [a, b] is smaller than [c, d] if b - a < d - c, or if the lengths are equal and a < c. Return [lo, hi]. 1 <= k <= 3500, each list has up to 50 numbers, values are between -10^5 and 10^5.
hint: Take one number from each list. Their min and max define a range. How can you move to a better choice by advancing only one list?
approach: Start with the first number of every list. The range of this choice is from the smallest chosen to the largest chosen. To get a better range, the smallest number must change, because moving anything else cannot shrink the range. So we keep the chosen numbers in a min-heap while tracking the current maximum. Each step: look at the range [heap min, current max], and remember it if it is smaller than the best so far. Then pop the minimum, and replace it with the next number from the same list (updating the maximum). If that list is exhausted we stop, since no later choice can cover every list. Updating only for strictly smaller ranges means ties keep the smaller start.
complexity: O(N log k) time for N total numbers, O(k) space
followups: How would you solve it by merging all numbers into one sorted list with list labels and a sliding window?
What if lists are unsorted?
What if only m of the k lists need to be covered?

title: Target Sum
statement: Given an array of non-negative integers nums and an integer target, put a + or a - sign in front of every number and add them up. Return how many different sign assignments make the total equal to target. Two assignments are different if some number gets a different sign (zeros count: +0 and -0 are different). 1 <= nums.length <= 20, the sum of nums is at most 1000, and -1000 <= target <= 1000.
hint: The numbers with a + sign form a subset P and the others form a subset N. What do sum(P) - sum(N) = target and sum(P) + sum(N) = total say about sum(P)?
approach: Let total be the sum of nums. If P is the set of numbers that get a plus and N the set that gets a minus, then sum(P) - sum(N) = target and sum(P) + sum(N) = total. Adding the two equations gives sum(P) = (total + target) / 2. So the question becomes: how many subsets of nums have this exact sum? If |target| > total or (total + target) is odd, the answer is 0. Otherwise run a counting 0/1 knapsack: ways[s] is the number of subsets with sum s, ways[0] = 1, and for each number we update s from high to low (so each number is used once): ways[s] += ways[s - num]. Zeros double the counts, which matches the two signs.
complexity: O(n * S) time, O(S) space where S = (total + target) / 2
followups: How would you solve it with top-down recursion and a memo on (index, running sum)?
Why must the inner loop go from high to low?
What if numbers can be negative?

title: Coin Change II
statement: Given a target amount and a list of distinct coin values (each available in unlimited number), return how many different combinations of coins add up to exactly amount. Combinations are unordered, so {1,2} and {2,1} count as one. Return 0 if it cannot be done. amount is at most 5000 and there are up to 300 coin types.
hint: To count combinations rather than sequences, process one coin type at a time in the outer loop.
approach: Let ways[a] be the number of combinations that make amount a, with ways[0] = 1 (the empty combination). Handle the coin types one by one. For a coin c, go through amounts from c up to the target in increasing order and add ways[a - c] to ways[a]. After finishing coin c, ways[a] counts combinations that use only the coins processed so far. The increasing loop lets the same coin be used many times (unbounded knapsack). Because the coin loop is outermost, every combination is counted once in a fixed coin order. If the loops were swapped, [1,2] and [2,1] would both be counted, which solves a different problem (ordered sequences).
followups: Why does swapping the two loops count ordered sequences instead?
How would you also return one example combination?
What if each coin can be used only a limited number of times?

title: Perfect Squares
statement: Given a positive integer n, return the smallest count of perfect square numbers (1, 4, 9, 16, ...) that add up to n. A square may be used many times. 1 <= n <= 10^4.
hint: This is "minimum number of coins" where the coins are the squares.
approach: Let dp[i] be the least number of squares that sum to i, with dp[0] = 0. For each i from 1 to n, the last square used could be any j*j <= i, and then the rest i - j*j needs dp[i - j*j] squares. So dp[i] = 1 + min over j of dp[i - j*j]. Every positive integer is a sum of at most 4 squares (Lagrange's theorem), so the answer is never larger than 4, but the DP does not need that fact. This is the unbounded knapsack idea: the items are squares and we minimise the count. Time is n times sqrt(n), which is about one million steps for n = 10^4.
followups: How does BFS over remainders give the same answer?
Can you use the four-square and three-square theorems for an O(sqrt n) answer?
How would you return the actual squares used?

title: Last Stone Weight II
statement: You have a list of stone weights. In each turn, pick any two stones x <= y and smash them: if x == y both are destroyed, otherwise the stone of weight x is destroyed and y becomes y - x. After all turns at most one stone remains. Return the smallest possible weight of that last stone (0 if none remains). 1 <= stones.length <= 30, each weight is 1 to 100.
hint: Think of the final result as a sum with a plus or minus in front of every stone. This is like splitting the stones into two piles.
approach: Whatever order we smash in, the weight of the last stone is a signed sum: some stones count positively and the others negatively. That means we split the stones into two groups with sums A and B, and the final weight is |A - B|. To make it as small as possible, make the two groups as equal as possible. Let total be the sum of all stones. We find the largest subset sum s that does not exceed total / 2, using a 0/1 knapsack boolean table. Then the other group has total - s and the answer is total - 2*s. The table has at most 30 * 1500 states, which is small.
followups: How is this problem related to Partition Equal Subset Sum?
How would you reconstruct which stones go into each group?
How can you speed up the table with a bitset?

title: Ones and Zeroes
statement: You get an array strs of binary strings (made of 0 and 1) and two integers m and n. Find the size of the largest subset of strs that uses at most m zeros and at most n ones in total, counting every character of all chosen strings. Each string can be chosen once. Up to 600 strings, each up to 100 characters, and 1 <= m, n <= 100.
hint: Each string is an item with two weights: its zeros and its ones. The capacity has two dimensions too.
approach: This is a 0/1 knapsack with two capacities. Let dp[i][j] be the largest number of strings we can pick using at most i zeros and j ones. Start with all zeros. For each string with z zeros and o ones, go through the table from the largest i and j downward (so each string is used at most once) and set dp[i][j] = max(dp[i][j], dp[i - z][j - o] + 1), which says: either skip this string, or take it and spend z zeros and o ones. Going downward matters because it prevents using the same string twice. The answer is dp[m][n].
complexity: O(len(strs) * m * n) time, O(m * n) space
followups: Why must both loops run downward?
How would you solve it top-down with memoization on (index, zeros, ones)?
What if each string can be used any number of times?

title: Minimum Path Sum
statement: A grid of non-negative integers has m rows and n columns. Start at the top-left cell and walk to the bottom-right cell, moving only right or down. Return the smallest possible sum of the numbers on the cells you visit (including the first and last cell). 1 <= m, n <= 200.
hint: To reach a cell you must come from the cell above or the cell on the left. Which one is better?
approach: Let best[r][c] be the least sum of a path from the top-left corner to cell (r, c). A path arrives from above or from the left, so best[r][c] = grid[r][c] + min(best[r-1][c], best[r][c-1]). The first row and first column have only one possible predecessor. Filling the table row by row gives the answer in the last cell. Since a row only depends on the row above and the cell to the left, we can keep a single array of length n and update it in place, which cuts the memory from m*n to n. All numbers are non-negative, but the same DP also works with negative numbers, because moves only go right or down.
followups: How would you also return the path itself?
What if you can also move up and left? (Dijkstra)
How would you handle blocked cells?

title: Unique Paths II
statement: A robot starts at the top-left cell of an m x n grid and wants to reach the bottom-right cell, moving only right or down. Cells with value 1 are obstacles that the robot cannot enter; cells with 0 are free. Return the number of different paths from the start to the end. The answer fits in a 32-bit integer. 1 <= m, n <= 100.
hint: The number of ways to reach a cell is the sum of the ways to reach its upper and left neighbors, unless the cell is blocked.
approach: Let ways[r][c] be the number of paths that end at cell (r, c). A free cell can be entered from above or from the left, so ways[r][c] = ways[r-1][c] + ways[r][c-1]. A blocked cell has ways = 0, because no path can pass through it. The start cell has 1 way if it is free and 0 if it is blocked. We process the grid row by row with a single array of length n: for each cell, if it is an obstacle set the value to 0, otherwise add the value to its left (the value already stored from the row above is the upper neighbor). The answer is the last entry. If the start or the end is blocked, the answer is 0.
followups: How would you handle the case where the answer might overflow?
What if the robot may also move diagonally?
How would you count paths through a required checkpoint cell?

title: Triangle
statement: A triangle is given as a list of rows, where row i has i+1 integers. Starting at the top, you walk down one row at a time; from position j in a row you may move to position j or j+1 in the next row. Return the smallest possible sum of the numbers on a path from the top to the bottom row. Up to 200 rows, values between -10^4 and 10^4.
hint: Try working from the bottom row upward. What is the best sum starting from each cell down to the bottom?
approach: Define best[i][j] as the smallest path sum from cell (i, j) down to the bottom. For the last row it is just the cell value. For any higher row, from (i, j) we can go to (i+1, j) or (i+1, j+1), so best[i][j] = tri[i][j] + min(best[i+1][j], best[i+1][j+1]). Computing bottom-up, the answer is best[0][0], the top cell. We only need the row below, so one array of length equal to the last row is enough: copy the last row, then for each higher row overwrite it from left to right using the old neighbors. Going bottom-up avoids special cases at the edges of the triangle.
followups: How would you print the path that gives the minimum?
Why is the top-down version harder to write in O(n) space?
What if you may also move to j-1 in the row below?

title: Dungeon Game
statement: A knight starts at the top-left cell of a dungeon grid and must reach the princess in the bottom-right cell, moving only right or down. Each cell holds an integer: a negative number is a demon that takes that much health, a positive number is a potion that gives health, and 0 is empty. The knight dies if his health ever drops to 0 or below, including right after entering the last cell. Return the minimum starting health that lets him make it. 1 <= m, n <= 200, values between -1000 and 1000.
hint: Going forward from the start is hard because you do not know the health you need. Think backwards from the princess.
approach: A forward DP does not work, since the best path so far and the health needed later trade off against each other. Instead go backwards: need[r][c] is the least health the knight must have when he enters cell (r, c) to survive to the end. At the princess cell he must keep at least 1 health after it, so need = max(1, 1 - dungeon[r][c]). For other cells, he picks the better next cell (the smaller need), then need[r][c] = max(1, minNext - dungeon[r][c]). The max with 1 means a potion can never make the requirement lower than 1. The answer is need at the top-left cell. A single row array is enough because each cell only reads its right and lower neighbors.
followups: Why does a forward DP with (max health, current health) pairs fail?
Can you solve it with binary search on the starting health and a feasibility DP?
How would you recover the path the knight should take?

title: Distinct Subsequences
statement: Given two strings s and t, return the number of different ways to choose characters from s (keeping their order, but not necessarily adjacent) so that the chosen characters spell exactly t. Two ways are different if they use different index sets in s. Input: s and t, 0 <= length <= 1000. The answer fits in a 32-bit signed integer.
hint: Let ways[i][j] = number of ways the first i chars of s can form the first j chars of t. What happens when s[i-1] equals t[j-1]?
approach: Define ways[j] as the number of ways to build the first j characters of t from the part of s read so far. Start with ways[0] = 1, because the empty string can be built in exactly one way. For each character c of s, go through j from the end of t down to 1. If c equals t[j-1], then c can be used as the last character of the prefix, so we add ways[j-1] to ways[j]. Skipping c keeps the old ways[j], which is already stored. Going downwards stops a single character of s from being used twice in the same step. The answer is ways[t.length].
followups: How would you also return one of the matching index sets?
Why must the inner loop go from high j to low j when you use one row?
What if the answer can exceed 32 bits and you must return it modulo 1e9+7?

title: Interleaving String
statement: Given three strings s1, s2 and s3, decide whether s3 can be formed by interleaving s1 and s2. Interleaving means you take characters from s1 and s2 in turn (any number from one before switching), keeping the original order inside each string, and using every character exactly once. Input: three strings, each of length up to 100 (s3 up to 200). Output: true or false.
hint: If you have used i chars of s1 and j chars of s2, the next char of s3 to match is s3[i+j]. Which two moves are possible?
approach: Let ok[i][j] mean: the first i characters of s1 and the first j characters of s2 can interleave into the first i+j characters of s3. If the lengths do not add up, the answer is false straight away. The cell is true when either we reach it by taking s1[i-1] (ok[i-1][j] is true and s1[i-1] equals s3[i+j-1]) or by taking s2[j-1] (ok[i][j-1] is true and s2[j-1] equals s3[i+j-1]). Only the previous row is needed, so one array of size |s2|+1 is enough. This works because the last character of any valid interleaving must come from the end of s1 or the end of s2, so every valid path is covered.
followups: Can you do it with a BFS or DFS plus memo over (i, j)? Compare it with the table.
What if there are k strings to interleave instead of two?
Could the answer be computed in O(min(m, n)) extra space?

title: Shortest Common Supersequence
statement: Given two strings a and b, return a shortest string that has both a and b as subsequences. Many strings can be shortest, so to make the answer unique, return the lexicographically smallest shortest one. Input: two lowercase strings with length 1 to 1000. Output: the string.
hint: First compute the length of the best supersequence for every pair of suffixes. Then walk forward and rebuild it.
approach: Let len[i][j] be the length of the shortest common supersequence of the suffixes a[i..] and b[j..]. If one suffix is empty, the answer is the length of the other. If a[i] equals b[j], the two characters can be shared, so len = 1 + len[i+1][j+1]. Otherwise we must spend one character on either a[i] or b[j], so len = 1 + min(len[i+1][j], len[i][j+1]). To rebuild, start at (0, 0). When the characters are equal, output one copy and move both. When they differ, move toward the smaller length; if both moves give the same length, output the smaller of the two characters, which makes the result lexicographically smallest. When one string ends, append the rest of the other.
followups: How is this related to the length of the longest common subsequence?
Can the reconstruction be done by walking back from the end of the table instead?
How would you extend this to three strings?

title: Delete Operation for Two Strings
statement: Given two strings word1 and word2, return the minimum number of single-character deletions (from either string) needed to make the two strings equal. Input: two lowercase strings, each of length up to 500. Output: the number of deletions.
hint: What is left after all the deletions? It is a string common to both words, in the same order.
approach: After the deletions, both strings become the same string, and that string is a subsequence of each original word. To delete as little as possible, we want to keep as many characters as possible, so the kept string should be a longest common subsequence (LCS). Every character not in the LCS must be deleted, so the answer is (|word1| - LCS) + (|word2| - LCS). The LCS is found with the standard table: if two characters match we extend the diagonal value by one, otherwise we take the best of dropping one character from either word. One rolling row keeps the memory small.
followups: How does this differ from Edit Distance, where replacements are allowed?
Can you print one of the resulting equal strings?
What if deleting a character from word1 cost more than from word2?

title: Palindromic Substrings
statement: Given a string s, count how many of its substrings are palindromes (read the same forwards and backwards). Substrings at different positions count separately, even if they have the same letters. Input: a string of length 1 to 1000. Output: the count.
hint: A palindrome is built from the middle outward. How many possible middles does a string of length n have?
approach: Every palindrome has a centre: either one character (odd length) or the gap between two characters (even length). That gives 2n - 1 centres. For each centre, expand outward while the two outer characters are equal; every successful expansion is one new palindromic substring, so we add one to the count each time. This is the interval view in disguise: substring [l, r] is a palindrome if s[l] equals s[r] and [l+1, r-1] is a palindrome. Expanding from the centre walks exactly through these nested intervals without needing an n by n table, so memory stays constant.
followups: Can you solve it in O(n) with Manacher's algorithm?
How would the table version dp[l][r] work, and what order fills it?
How would you return the longest palindromic substring instead?

title: Longest Palindromic Subsequence
statement: Given a string s, return the length of the longest palindromic subsequence: the longest sequence of characters taken from s in order (not necessarily next to each other) that reads the same in both directions. Input: a string of length 1 to 1000. Output: the length.
hint: Look at the two ends of the interval [i, j]. If they match, they can wrap a palindrome inside. If not, one of them is useless.
approach: Let best[i][j] be the longest palindromic subsequence inside s[i..j]. A single character has length 1. If s[i] equals s[j], we can use both as the outer pair, so best[i][j] = best[i+1][j-1] + 2. If they differ, at most one of them can be in the answer, so best[i][j] = max(best[i+1][j], best[i][j-1]). Intervals depend on shorter intervals, so we fill i from the end of the string to the start and j from i+1 to the end; a rolling row keeps only the dependency on row i+1 and the current row. The answer is best[0][n-1].
followups: It equals the LCS of s and reverse(s). Why?
How would you reconstruct the subsequence itself?
What is the minimum number of insertions to make s a palindrome?

title: Burst Balloons
statement: You have balloons in a row, each with a number. Bursting balloon i earns nums[i-1] * nums[i] * nums[i+1] coins, where a missing neighbour (off either end) counts as 1. After a balloon bursts, its neighbours become adjacent. Return the maximum coins you can collect by bursting all balloons in the best order. Input: an array of up to 300 integers in 0..100.
hint: Do not choose the first balloon to burst. Choose the LAST balloon to burst in an interval. Then its neighbours are fixed.
approach: Pad the array with a 1 on each side. Let best[l][r] be the most coins from bursting every balloon strictly between l and r. Think about which balloon k in that range is burst last. At that moment only l and r remain around it, so it earns pad[l] * pad[k] * pad[r]. The balloons left of k and right of k were burst earlier and do not affect each other, because k is still standing between them, so those two parts are independent sub-problems: best[l][k] and best[k][r]. Take the maximum over k. Fill by increasing gap size. Choosing the last balloon is the trick that makes the sub-problems independent.
followups: Why does "burst first" fail to split the problem into independent parts?
Can you recover the actual bursting order?
How does this relate to matrix-chain multiplication?

title: Minimum Cost Tree From Leaf Values
statement: You are given an array arr of positive integers. Build any binary tree where every node has 0 or 2 children, the leaves in left-to-right order are exactly arr, and each non-leaf node's value is the product of the largest leaf in its left subtree and the largest leaf in its right subtree. The cost of a tree is the sum of its non-leaf node values. Return the minimum possible cost. Input: array of length 2..40 with values 1..15.
hint: Pick the point k where the interval is split into a left subtree and a right subtree. The root costs max(left) * max(right).
approach: The leaves keep their order, so each subtree covers a contiguous interval [i, j] of arr. Let cost[i][j] be the minimum cost to build a tree on that interval, and big[i][j] the maximum value in it. A single leaf costs 0. For a longer interval, try every split k between i and j: the left subtree uses [i, k], the right uses [k+1, j], and the root adds big[i][k] * big[k+1][j]. So cost[i][j] is the minimum over k of cost[i][k] + cost[k+1][j] + big[i][k] * big[k+1][j]. Shorter intervals are solved first. The maximum values do not depend on the tree shape, so the two parts are independent.
followups: A monotonic stack solves it in O(n). What is the greedy idea?
Why is the maximum of a subtree independent of the tree shape?
How would you build the optimal tree, not only the cost?

title: House Robber III
statement: The houses form a binary tree, and each node holds the money in that house. You cannot rob two houses that are directly linked (a parent and its child). Return the maximum money you can rob. Input: the tree as a level-order array with null for missing children (0 to 10000 nodes, values 0..10000). Output: the maximum amount.
hint: For each node, keep two answers: the best if you rob this node, and the best if you skip it.
approach: Walk the tree bottom-up (post-order). For every node return a pair: [rob, skip]. If we rob the node, we cannot rob its children, so rob = node value + skip(left) + skip(right). If we skip the node, each child is free to be robbed or not, so skip = max(rob, skip) of the left child + max(rob, skip) of the right child. An empty child gives [0, 0]. The answer is the larger value of the pair at the root. Returning a pair avoids recomputing the same subtrees, which a plain recursion with two choices would do many times. The array input is first converted into linked nodes; the recursion is written with an explicit order to avoid deep call stacks on long chains.
followups: Why does a single value per node (no pair) not work?
How would the answer change if you could not rob a grandparent and grandchild either?
Can you print which houses are robbed?

title: Binary Tree Cameras
statement: You are given a binary tree. A camera placed on a node watches that node, its parent and its children. Return the minimum number of cameras needed so that every node is watched. Input: the tree as a level-order array with null for missing children (1 to 1000 nodes; the values are ignored). Output: the number of cameras.
hint: Give each node one of three states: has a camera, is watched without a camera, or is not watched yet.
approach: Process nodes from the leaves up. Each node returns one of three states: 0 = not covered, 1 = has a camera, 2 = covered without a camera. A missing child counts as covered (2). If any child is not covered, this node must hold a camera, so we count one and return 1. Else if any child has a camera, this node is covered by it, so return 2. Otherwise both children are covered but have no camera, so this node is not covered yet; return 0 and let its parent deal with it. This is greedy: it is always better to put a camera on the parent of an uncovered node than on the node itself, because the parent also covers more. If the root is still uncovered at the end, add one more camera.
followups: Can you prove the greedy rule (camera on the parent of an uncovered node) is optimal?
How would a DP with three values per node give the same answer?
What changes if a camera only watches its children and itself?

title: Unique Binary Search Trees
statement: Given n, return how many structurally different binary search trees can store exactly the values 1..n. Two trees are different if their shapes are different. Input: an integer n from 1 to 19. Output: the count.
hint: Pick which value is the root. The smaller values must all go left and the larger values all go right.
approach: Let count[k] be the number of BST shapes with k nodes; count[0] = 1 for the empty tree. If we choose value r as the root of a tree with k nodes, then r - 1 smaller values go to the left subtree and k - r larger values go to the right subtree. The left and right shapes are chosen independently, so the number of trees with that root is count[r-1] * count[k-r]. Summing over every possible root r from 1 to k gives count[k]. Only the number of nodes matters, not the actual values, because any set of consecutive ranks forms the same shapes. These numbers are the Catalan numbers: 1, 1, 2, 5, 14, 42, and so on.
followups: Is there a closed formula? (Catalan: C(2n, n) / (n + 1).)
How would you list all the trees instead of counting them?
How many trees if the tree were not a search tree but any binary tree shape?

title: Longest ZigZag Path in a Binary Tree
statement: In a binary tree, a zigzag path starts at any node, picks a direction (left or right), moves to that child, then switches direction at every step (left, right, left, ... or right, left, right, ...) until it cannot continue. Its length is the number of edges. Return the length of the longest zigzag path. Input: the tree as a level-order array with null for missing children (1 to 50000 nodes). Output: the length.
hint: For each node, store the longest zigzag that arrives there by going left, and the longest that arrives there by going right.
approach: For each node keep two numbers: goLeft = the longest zigzag path that starts at this node and goes to the left child first, and goRight, the same but starting to the right. If the left child exists, goLeft = 1 + (the child's goRight), because after going left the path must turn right. Likewise goRight = 1 + (the right child's goLeft). A missing child gives 0. These values come from the children, so we compute them bottom-up and keep the maximum of all of them. Using a level-order array, children always have larger indices than their parent after conversion, so a simple reverse loop works and no recursion is needed.
followups: How would you also return the path itself?
What if a path may bend at most twice?
Can you do it with a DFS that carries the current zigzag length down instead?

title: Longest Increasing Path in a Matrix
statement: Given an m x n grid of integers, find the length of the longest path in which every next cell has a strictly larger value than the previous one. You may move up, down, left or right (no diagonals) and may not leave the grid. Input: the grid, with 1 <= m, n <= 200. Output: the number of cells on the longest path.
hint: A step always goes to a strictly larger value, so there are no cycles. Store, for every cell, the longest path that starts there.
approach: Think of each cell as a node with arrows to its neighbours that have larger values. Because values strictly increase along an arrow, the graph has no cycle (a DAG). Let longest[cell] be the longest increasing path starting at that cell. It equals 1 plus the maximum of longest[] over the larger neighbours, or 1 if there is none. Compute it with DFS and memoization: the first time a cell is visited we compute and store its value, and later visits reuse it, so each cell is solved once. Take the maximum over all cells. This is "memoized DFS where the transition looks at up to four neighbours", unlike the fixed-step DP of climbing stairs.
complexity: O(m * n) time, O(m * n) space
followups: How would you solve it without recursion, using a topological order (Kahn's algorithm on in-degrees)?
What if equal values were allowed to continue the path?
Why can recursion depth become a problem, and how do you avoid it?

title: Longest String Chain
statement: A word A is a predecessor of word B if you can insert exactly one letter anywhere in A (without reordering the others) to get B. A word chain is a sequence of words where each word is a predecessor of the next. Given a list of words, return the length of the longest possible chain using words from the list. A single word is a chain of length 1. Input: 1 to 1000 lowercase words, each of length 1 to 16. Output: the length.
hint: Sort words by length. For each word, try deleting each letter and look up the shorter word in a map.
approach: Words can only link to words that are exactly one letter longer, so if we process words from shortest to longest, every possible predecessor of a word has already been handled. Keep a map chain[word] = longest chain that ends at that word. For a new word w, try removing each of its letters one at a time; if the shorter string exists in the map, then chain[w] can be chain[shorter] + 1. Take the best over all deletions (or 1 if none exist). The answer is the maximum value in the map. Checking predecessors by deletion costs about L tries of length L each, which is far cheaper than comparing the word with every shorter word. The word graph is a DAG ordered by length.
complexity: O(n log n + n * L^2) time, O(n * L) space
followups: What if words could also be linked by replacing one letter?
How would you print the chain itself?
Could you avoid sorting by using a DFS with memoization on the predecessor map?

title: Largest Divisible Subset
statement: Given a set of distinct positive integers, find the largest subset in which every pair (a, b) satisfies a % b == 0 or b % a == 0. Return the subset sorted in increasing order. If several subsets have the maximum size, any is accepted by the original problem; the tests here use inputs with a single answer. Input: 1 to 1000 distinct integers in 1..2^31 - 1.
hint: Sort the numbers. If a divides b and b divides c, then a divides c, so you only need to check the neighbouring pair in a chain.
approach: Sort the numbers ascending. In a valid subset sorted the same way, divisibility is transitive: if each element divides the next one, then each element divides all later ones. So a valid subset is just a chain in which every element divides the next. Let size[i] be the length of the longest chain ending at nums[i], and prev[i] the index before it. For each i, look at all earlier j and, if nums[i] % nums[j] == 0, consider size[j] + 1. Keep the best j. The graph with arrows from divisors to multiples is a DAG, and this is a longest-path computation on it. At the end, follow the prev links from the index with the largest size to rebuild the subset, and reverse it.
followups: How would you speed this up when values are small, using multiples of each number?
Why is checking only the previous element of the chain enough?
What if the numbers were not distinct?

title: Partition Array for Maximum Sum
statement: Split an integer array into contiguous parts, each of length at most k. After the split, every element in a part is replaced by the largest value in that part. Return the largest possible sum of the array after this change. Input: array arr of 1 to 500 integers in 0..1e9 and an integer k from 1 to the length of arr. Output: the maximum sum (fits in 32-bit).
hint: Let best[i] be the answer for the first i elements. What is the last part, and how long can it be?
approach: Let best[i] be the maximum sum for the first i elements. The last part is arr[i-len .. i-1] for some length len from 1 to k. After replacing, that part contributes len times its maximum. The elements before it form an independent smaller problem with value best[i-len]. So best[i] = max over len of best[i-len] + len * max(last len elements). While we increase len, we keep a running maximum of the part. best[0] = 0, and the answer is best[n]. Every state looks back at up to k earlier states, so the transition is not a constant number of steps, but each state depends only on earlier ones, which is the shape of a DAG.
followups: Can a monotonic deque make it O(n)?
How would you recover the actual partition?
What if each part also had a minimum length?

title: Shortest Path Visiting All Nodes
statement: You have an undirected, connected graph with n nodes labelled 0..n-1, given as a list of edges [a, b]. Find the length (number of edges) of the shortest walk that visits every node at least once. You may start at any node and may revisit nodes and reuse edges. Input: n (1 to 12) and the edge list. Output: the length of the shortest walk.
hint: The state is not just the current node. It also includes which nodes were already visited, which you can store as a bitmask.
approach: Use breadth-first search over states (node, visitedMask), where visitedMask has bit i set if node i has been visited. All edges cost 1, so BFS finds the shortest walk. Start from every node at once: for each node i, the state (i, 1 << i) is at distance 0. From a state, moving along an edge to neighbour v gives (v, mask | 1 << v) at distance +1. The first time we pop a state whose mask has all n bits set, its distance is the answer. There are only n * 2^n states, at most 12 * 4096, and each state is visited once thanks to a seen table. A plain graph search without the mask would stop early and could not tell whether all nodes were covered.
complexity: O(2^n * n * deg) time, O(2^n * n) space
followups: Why is BFS (not Dijkstra) enough here?
How does this differ from the travelling salesman problem, where each node is visited once?
How could you reduce memory by pruning symmetric states?

title: Partition to K Equal Sum Subsets
statement: Given an array of positive integers nums and an integer k, decide whether the array can be split into k non-empty groups whose sums are all equal, using every number exactly once. Input: nums with 1 to 16 elements (each 1..10000) and k from 1 to the length of nums. Output: true or false.
hint: If the total is not divisible by k, stop. Otherwise each group must sum to total / k. Track which numbers are used with a bitmask.
approach: Let target = total / k. If the total is not divisible by k or some number exceeds target, the answer is false. Let fill[mask] be the sum of the numbers in mask, taken modulo target, or -1 if the mask cannot be reached by filling groups one after another. This works because we always finish one group before starting the next, so the leftover of the current group is just (sum of used numbers) mod target. Start with fill[0] = 0. For each reachable mask and each unused number x, if fill[mask] + x <= target, then mask | (1 << x) is reachable with value (fill[mask] + x) % target. If the full mask is reachable, the partition exists. There are only 2^16 masks, so this is fast.
followups: A backtracking search with sorting and pruning also works. When is it faster than the mask?
What if numbers could be negative or zero?
How would you return the groups themselves?

title: Smallest Sufficient Team
statement: A project needs a list of required skills. You have a list of people, and each person knows some of the skills. A team is sufficient if for every required skill at least one team member has it. Return the indices of a smallest sufficient team, sorted in increasing order. Several smallest teams may exist and the original problem accepts any; the tests here only use inputs with a single smallest team. Input: reqSkills (1 to 16 distinct strings) and people (1 to 60 lists of skills). Output: the sorted list of indices.
hint: Give each required skill a bit. A person is then a bitmask, and a team is the OR of its members.
approach: Map every required skill to a bit, so each person becomes a mask of the skills they cover. Let team[mask] be the smallest list of people whose combined skills equal exactly this set. Start with team[0] = []. For every person p, and for every mask already reachable, the new mask = mask | person[p] can be reached by adding p. If the new mask has no team yet, or the new team is smaller, store it. Process the people one by one and loop over a snapshot of the masks, so a person is used at most once. The answer is team[fullMask]. A set-cover problem is hard in general, but there are only 2^16 skill sets, so the state space is small.
complexity: O(people * 2^skills) time, O(2^skills * team size) space
followups: Why can a greedy "pick the person who covers most uncovered skills" fail?
How would you count all smallest teams?
How does the solution change when each person has a cost and you minimise total cost?

title: Number of Ways to Wear Different Hats to Each Other
statement: There are n people (n <= 10) and 40 types of hats labelled 1..40. hats[i] is the list of hat types person i likes. Each person must wear exactly one hat they like, and no two people may wear the same type of hat. Return the number of ways, modulo 1,000,000,007. Input: hats, a list of n lists (each with 1 to 40 distinct values). Output: the count modulo 1e9+7.
hint: There are many more hats (40) than people (10). Iterate over hats and keep a bitmask of which people already have a hat.
approach: Flip the point of view: instead of choosing a hat for each person, decide for each hat type whether it goes to one person or to nobody. First build, for each hat, the list of people who like it. Let ways[mask] be the number of ways in which exactly the people in mask have received distinct hats using the hat types processed so far. Start with ways[0] = 1. For each hat type h, go through masks from high to low (so the hat is used at most once), and for every person p who likes h and is not in mask, add ways[mask] to ways[mask | 1 << p]. The answer is ways[full] after all 40 hats. The mask has only 2^10 values, and the loop over hats is 40, which is much smaller than 40^10.
followups: Why is iterating over people (10! orders of hats) not feasible but iterating over hats is?
Why must the mask loop go from high to low?
How would you count the ways if two people could share a hat type?

title: Range Sum Query - Mutable
statement: Design NumArray(nums) which stores an integer array and supports two operations: update(index, val) sets nums[index] to val, and sumRange(left, right) returns the sum of nums[left..right] (both ends included). Input: a list of operation names and a list of argument lists (the constructor gets [nums]). Return a list with null for NumArray and update, and the sum for sumRange. Up to 30000 elements and 30000 operations.
hint: A prefix sum array makes queries O(1) but updates O(n). A tree over the array makes both O(log n).
approach: Store the array in a Fenwick tree (binary indexed tree), a compact structure where position i stores the sum of a block of elements whose size is the lowest set bit of i. To get the prefix sum up to i, repeatedly add tree[i] and then remove the lowest set bit of i (i -= i & -i). To add a delta at position i, update tree[i] and then move up with i += i & -i. An update to a new value is an add of the difference between the new and old value, so we keep a copy of the raw array too. A range sum is prefix(right) - prefix(left - 1). Both operations touch only O(log n) cells. A segment tree gives the same bounds and extends to min, max and other combiners.
complexity: O(n) build, O(log n) per update and per query
followups: When is a plain prefix-sum array better than a Fenwick tree?
How would you support range updates (add v to all of nums[l..r])?
How would the structure change if sumRange had to return the maximum instead?

title: Count of Smaller Numbers After Self
statement: Given an integer array nums, return an array counts where counts[i] is the number of elements to the right of position i that are strictly smaller than nums[i]. Input: nums with 1 to 100000 integers in -10000..10000. Output: the array counts.
hint: Go from right to left. For each number, you need "how many smaller numbers have I already inserted?"
approach: Walk the array from the last element to the first. Keep a Fenwick tree indexed by value rank, where position r holds how many of the numbers seen so far have rank r. For nums[i], the answer is the number of seen values with a strictly smaller rank, which is a prefix sum query on the tree up to rank - 1. Then insert nums[i] by adding one at its rank. To keep the tree small, replace values by their rank among the sorted distinct values (coordinate compression). Because we only insert elements that are to the right of i, the query sees exactly the elements after position i. Each step costs O(log n), so the total is O(n log n), much better than comparing every pair.
complexity: O(n log n) time, O(n) space
followups: Can you solve it with merge sort instead? What is counted during the merge?
What if you need counts of larger numbers, or equal numbers?
Why do we need coordinate compression when values can be huge?

title: Count of Range Sum
statement: Given an integer array nums and two integers lower and upper, count the subarrays (contiguous, non-empty) whose sum is between lower and upper, both included. Input: nums with 1 to 100000 integers (absolute value up to 2^31) and lower <= upper. Output: the number of such subarrays.
hint: Use prefix sums. A subarray sum is prefix[j] - prefix[i]. For each j, count earlier i whose prefix lies in a window.
approach: Let prefix[0] = 0 and prefix[k] = sum of the first k numbers. The subarray from i to j-1 has sum prefix[j] - prefix[i], so we count pairs i < j with lower <= prefix[j] - prefix[i] <= upper. For a fixed j this means prefix[i] lies in [prefix[j] - upper, prefix[j] - lower]. Sort prefix sums by merge sort. When merging two sorted halves, every left value is paired with every right value, and because both halves are sorted, the matching range in the right half moves only forward, so two pointers count all pairs in linear time. The index order is already respected because left-half indices are smaller than right-half indices. The recursion depth is log n.
complexity: O(n log n) time, O(n) space
followups: How would a Fenwick tree over compressed prefix sums solve this?
Why does the merge need the left half to be sorted before counting?
What changes if you only need to know whether any such subarray exists?

title: Falling Squares
statement: Squares fall one at a time onto a number line. The i-th square is described by [left, size]: it occupies the interval [left, left + size) on the x-axis and is dropped from above. It falls until its bottom touches the x-axis or the top of a square that overlaps it (touching only at an edge does not count). After each drop, report the height of the tallest stack so far. Input: positions, 1 to 1000 pairs with left in 1..1e8 and size in 1..1e6. Output: list of the maximum height after each square.
hint: A new square lands on the maximum height among the positions it covers. Then it sets all those positions to its own top height.
approach: Only the squares' edges matter, so compress the x-coordinates: collect all left and right edges, sort and de-duplicate them. Cells between neighbouring coordinates then have a single height each. Keep an array height[] over these cells. For a new square covering cells [a, b), the landing level is the maximum of height[a..b-1]; its top is level + size; then assign that top to every cell in [a, b). The running maximum of all tops is the answer after this drop. With at most 2000 coordinates and 1000 squares, scanning the range directly is fast enough. For much larger inputs, the "range maximum query plus range assign" would be handled by a segment tree with lazy propagation in O(log n) per drop.
complexity: O(n^2) time with a plain scan, O(n log n) with a lazy segment tree
followups: How does a lazy segment tree support range assign and range max together?
Can a sorted list of disjoint intervals (like an interval map) also work?
What if squares could also be removed?

title: The Skyline Problem
statement: Each building is [left, right, height]: a rectangle sitting on the ground from x = left to x = right. Return the skyline formed by all buildings: a list of key points [x, height], sorted by x, where each key point is the left end of a horizontal segment of the outline. The last point has height 0 and marks where the last building ends. Consecutive key points must not have the same height. Input: buildings sorted by left, up to 10000 buildings, coordinates up to 2^31 - 1. Output: the key points.
hint: The skyline of one building is two points. Can you merge the skylines of two halves, like in merge sort?
approach: Split the buildings into two halves, solve each recursively, and merge the two skylines. A skyline of one building is [[left, height], [right, 0]]. To merge two skylines, walk through both lists by x. Keep the current height of each skyline (h1 and h2), starting at 0. At every key point take the one with the smaller x (or both if they are equal), update that skyline's height, and the merged height at x is max(h1, h2). Add [x, max] to the result only if it differs from the last height added, which removes redundant points. Each merge is linear, and there are log n levels, so the total cost is O(n log n). The same idea as merge sort works because the merged outline only depends on the two sub-outlines.
complexity: O(n log n) time, O(n) space
followups: How does the sweep-line solution with a max-heap compare?
Why must adjacent key points with equal height be removed?
How would you handle buildings that are not sorted by left?

title: Median of Two Sorted Arrays
statement: Given two sorted arrays nums1 and nums2, return the median of all their elements combined (the middle value, or the average of the two middle values when the total is even). The running time should be logarithmic in the size of the arrays. Input: two sorted arrays with total length 1 to 2000 (one may be empty), values in -1e6..1e6. Output: the median as a number.
hint: You do not need to merge. Find a cut in each array so that the left parts together hold exactly half of all elements, and every left element is <= every right element.
approach: Take the shorter array A and the longer B. A cut at position i in A (i elements on the left) forces a cut at j = half - i in B, where half = (total + 1) / 2 rounded down, so the combined left side has exactly half of the elements. The cut is correct when the largest element on the left of A is <= the smallest on the right of B, and the largest on the left of B is <= the smallest on the right of A. If A's left maximum is too big, move the cut in A to the left; otherwise move it to the right. This is a binary search over i, so it takes O(log min(m, n)). Missing sides count as minus or plus infinity. At the correct cut, the median is the left maximum (odd total) or the average of the left maximum and right minimum (even total).
followups: How would you find the k-th smallest element of two sorted arrays?
Why do we binary search on the shorter array?
What if there are k sorted arrays?

title: Reverse Pairs
statement: Count the pairs of positions (i, j) with i < j such that nums[i] > 2 * nums[j]. Input: array nums with 1 to 50000 integers between -2^31 and 2^31 - 1. Output: the number of such pairs. (Use arithmetic that does not overflow 32 bits.)
hint: Count the pairs between the two halves of a merge sort before you merge them.
approach: Use merge sort. Split the array into a left half and a right half and count the pairs inside each recursively. Now count the pairs that cross the halves: i in the left, j in the right. Both halves are already sorted after the recursive calls, so for each left value x (moving upward), the set of right values y with x > 2 * y only grows as x grows. A single pointer on the right half moves forward while 2 * right[pointer] < x and gives the count for every x without restarting. Add the pointer offset to the answer. After counting, merge the two halves as normal so the parent can use the sorted result. Counting is separate from merging because the condition (twice the value) is different from the sort order.
complexity: O(n log n) time, O(n) space
followups: How would a Fenwick tree over compressed values solve it?
Why is it unsafe to compute 2 * nums[j] in 32-bit integers?
How does this relate to counting inversions?

title: Different Ways to Add Parentheses
statement: Given a string made of non-negative integers and the operators +, - and *, return the results of every distinct way of grouping the numbers and operators with parentheses. Different groupings that give the same value are listed once per grouping, so the result can contain duplicates. The order of the results does not matter. Input: expression of length 1 to 20, numbers 0..99. Output: the list of values.
hint: Choose the operator that is evaluated last. Everything to its left and right is a smaller problem of the same kind.
approach: For every operator in the expression, treat it as the last one to be applied. The part before it and the part after it are smaller expressions that can be grouped in any way. Solve both recursively to get a list of possible values for the left and a list for the right. Then combine every left value with every right value using this operator, and add the results to the answer. If the expression has no operator, it is a single number and the only result is that number. Different choices of the last operator and different sub-groupings give all possible parenthesizations. The same substring appears many times in the recursion, so cache the results by substring (memoization) to avoid repeated work.
complexity: Catalan-number many results; O(C(n)) time for n operators, with memo each substring is solved once
followups: How many results are there for k operators? (Catalan numbers.)
How would you return the parenthesized strings instead of the values?
Can you do it bottom-up with a table indexed by operand ranges?

title: Car Pooling
statement: A car drives in one direction and has capacity empty seats. Each trip is [passengers, from, to]: that many people get in at position from and get out at position to. Decide whether the car can carry every trip without ever holding more than capacity people. People leaving at a position make room before people boarding at the same position. Input: trips (1 to 1000) with from < to <= 1000, and capacity. Output: true or false.
hint: Turn each trip into two events: +passengers at from and -passengers at to. Sweep through the events in order and track the load.
approach: The number of people in the car only changes at pick-up and drop-off points. Create an event for each trip: (from, +passengers) and (to, -passengers). Sort events by position; if two events share a position, put the drop-offs (negative values) first, because people leave before others board. Then sweep through the sorted events while adding each change to a running load. If at any moment the load goes above capacity, the answer is false. If we finish the sweep without exceeding capacity, the answer is true. Checking only after each event is enough, because the load is constant between events. A difference array over positions 0..1000 works equally well when coordinates are small.
complexity: O(n log n) time, O(n) space
followups: Solve it with a difference array when positions are at most 1000.
What if you had to return the earliest position where the car overflows?
How does this relate to Meeting Rooms II?

title: My Calendar II
statement: Design MyCalendarTwo, a calendar that allows double bookings but not triple bookings. book(start, end) tries to add the half-open event [start, end). It succeeds (returns true) and stores the event only if it does not make any moment covered by three events; otherwise it returns false and stores nothing. Input: a list of operation names and a list of argument lists. Return null for the constructor and the true/false result for each book call. At most 1000 calls.
hint: Keep a map of change points: +1 where an event starts, -1 where it ends. Sweep in order and check the running count never reaches 3.
approach: Store the calendar as a map from time to the change in the number of active events: +1 at each start and -1 at each end. To test a new event, first add its two change points tentatively. Then sweep through all points in increasing time order while keeping a running sum; the running sum is the number of events active right after that time. If the sum ever reaches 3, the new event would create a triple booking, so undo the two changes and return false. Otherwise keep them and return true. Because end times are exclusive, an event ending at t and another starting at t do not overlap; in the sweep the -1 and +1 at the same time are merged in one map entry, so the sum is correct. Sorting the keys on each call costs O(n log n).
complexity: O(n log n) per booking, O(n) space
followups: What if triple bookings were allowed but quadruple ones were not (My Calendar III asks for the maximum overlap)?
How would a balanced tree or segment tree improve the cost per booking?
Why must a failed booking leave no trace?

title: Corporate Flight Bookings
statement: There are n flights labelled 1..n. Each booking is [first, last, seats]: it reserves that many seats on every flight from first to last, both included. Return an array answer of length n where answer[i] is the total number of seats reserved on flight i + 1. Input: n up to 20000 and up to 20000 bookings. Output: the array.
hint: Do not add seats to every flight in the range. Mark only where the range starts and where it stops, then take a running sum.
approach: A difference array stores how much the answer changes from one flight to the next instead of the answer itself. For a booking [first, last, seats], add seats at index first, and subtract seats at index last + 1, because the booking no longer applies after flight last. All bookings are marked in O(1) each. Then the real value for flight i is the prefix sum of the difference array up to i. This works because adding to a range equals adding to the starting point of the difference and removing it right after the end point; the prefix sum spreads the amount over exactly the range. The array has one extra slot at the end to hold the last subtraction safely.
followups: How would you extend it to a 2-D grid of updates?
What if you needed to answer prefix queries between updates?
Why does the array need n + 2 slots?

title: Rectangle Area II
statement: Each rectangle is [x1, y1, x2, y2], the bottom-left and top-right corners of an axis-aligned rectangle. Rectangles may overlap. Return the total area covered by the union of all rectangles (overlap counted once), modulo 1,000,000,007. Input: 1 to 200 rectangles with coordinates 0..1e9. Output: the area modulo 1e9+7.
hint: Cut the plane into vertical strips between consecutive x-coordinates. In each strip, the covered height is the union of the y-ranges of rectangles that span it.
approach: Collect every x1 and x2, sort and remove duplicates. Between two neighbouring x values, the picture does not change horizontally, so the strip behaves like a one-dimensional problem. For each strip, take the rectangles that cover the whole strip (x1 <= left edge and x2 >= right edge), sort their y-ranges and compute the length of their union by walking through them and tracking the highest end seen so far. The area of the strip is (union length) * (strip width). Add up all strips. The product can reach 1e18, which is beyond exact JavaScript numbers, so use BigInt for the sum and take the modulo at the end. With n rectangles there are at most 2n strips and each costs O(n log n).
complexity: O(n^2 log n) time, O(n) space
followups: How does a segment tree over y-coordinates bring the cost down to O(n log n)?
Why do we need BigInt here?
How would you compute the perimeter of the union instead?

title: Meeting Rooms
statement: Given a list of meeting time intervals [start, end], decide whether one person can attend all of them. A meeting ending at time t and another starting at time t do not conflict. Input: up to 10000 intervals with 0 <= start < end <= 1e6 (the list may be empty). Output: true if there are no overlapping meetings, otherwise false.
hint: After sorting by start time, only neighbours can overlap.
approach: Sort the meetings by start time. Now if any two meetings overlap, then some two neighbouring meetings overlap: suppose meeting A starts before B and they overlap, then every meeting between them in sorted order starts after A and before the end of A, so it overlaps A (or the pair next to it) too. So we only compare each meeting with the previous one: if the start of the current meeting is earlier than the end of the previous meeting, there is an overlap and the answer is false. Because an end time equal to the next start is allowed, the check uses a strict "less than". If no neighbouring pair overlaps, the answer is true.
complexity: O(n log n) time, O(1) extra space
followups: How would you find the minimum number of rooms (Meeting Rooms II)?
Can you detect the overlap without sorting if times are small integers?
Which two meetings conflict? Return one such pair.

title: Interval List Intersections
statement: You are given two lists of closed intervals [start, end]. Each list is sorted and its own intervals do not overlap. Return the intersection of the two lists as a sorted list of intervals. A single point such as [5, 5] counts as an interval. Input: two lists, each with up to 1000 intervals, values 0..1e9. Output: the list of intersections.
hint: Use two pointers. Compare the current interval of each list, record their overlap if any, and move past the one that ends first.
approach: Keep a pointer i on the first list and j on the second. For the current pair, the overlap starts at the larger of the two starts and ends at the smaller of the two ends. If start <= end, the pair really intersects, so record [start, end]. Then decide which pointer to advance: the interval that ends first cannot intersect with anything further in the other list, because the other list's next intervals start after the current one ends, and the current one finished earlier. So move the pointer of the interval with the smaller end; if both end together, advancing either one is safe. The loop ends when either list is used up. Each step moves a pointer, so the work is linear.
complexity: O(m + n) time, O(1) extra space
followups: How would you intersect k sorted interval lists?
What if the intervals in a list could overlap each other?
How would you compute the union of the two lists?

title: Remove Covered Intervals
statement: An interval [a, b) is covered by [c, d) if c <= a and b <= d. Given a list of intervals [start, end), remove every interval that is covered by another interval in the list, and return how many intervals remain. Input: 1 to 1000 intervals with 0 <= start < end <= 100000, all distinct. Output: the number of remaining intervals.
hint: Sort by start ascending and, for equal starts, by end descending. Then track the largest end seen so far.
approach: Sort intervals by start ascending, and when starts are equal put the longer interval first (end descending). Go through the sorted list while remembering the largest end seen so far. For a new interval, if its end is less than or equal to that maximum, then an earlier interval started no later and ends no earlier, so it covers the current one and we skip it. Otherwise the current interval is not covered by anything before it, so we count it and update the maximum end. Intervals that come later in the order start no earlier, so they could only cover the current interval if they had the same start, which the descending end order handles by putting those first. One pass after sorting is enough.
complexity: O(n log n) time, O(1) extra space
followups: Why do ties on the start need the end in descending order?
How is this related to Non-overlapping Intervals?
Could you do it with a sweep over events instead of sorting intervals?

title: Employee Free Time
statement: schedule[i] is the list of working intervals [start, end] of employee i. Each employee's list is sorted and non-overlapping. Return the finite intervals of time during which every employee is free, in sorted order. Free time before the earliest start or after the latest end is infinite and is not reported, and zero-length gaps are not reported. Input: schedule with 1 to 50 employees, each with 1 to 50 intervals, values 0..1e8. Output: the list of common free intervals.
hint: Merge all the intervals of all employees into one busy timeline. The gaps between merged blocks are free for everyone.
approach: Someone is free at a time exactly when nobody is working. So put the working intervals of all employees into one list and sort it by start. Walk through it while maintaining the end of the current busy block. If the next interval starts after the current end, there is a gap [end, start] where no one works, so it is a free interval; record it. Then extend the current end to the larger of the two ends. If the next interval starts at or before the current end, it overlaps the block, so only the end is extended. Any gap found this way lies between two busy blocks, so it is finite, and the time before the first start and after the last end are never reported. Merging k sorted lists with a heap gives O(N log k) but sorting is simpler.
complexity: O(N log N) time for N intervals, O(N) space
followups: How would you do it with a min-heap over the k employees, without sorting everything?
What if you only wanted free slots at least d minutes long?
How would you also report time when at least one employee (not everyone) is free?

title: Count Primes
statement: Given a non-negative integer n, return how many prime numbers are strictly less than n. Input: n from 0 to 5,000,000. Output: the count.
hint: Do not test each number separately. Mark multiples of every prime you find as not prime (sieve of Eratosthenes).
approach: Make a boolean array where composite[i] says that i is not prime. Go through i from 2. If i is not yet marked, it is prime, so count it, and mark its multiples as composite. The marking can start at i * i, because every smaller multiple k * i with k < i has a smaller prime factor and was already marked by it. We only need to start marking while i * i < n. Every composite number is crossed off by its smallest prime factor, and the total number of marks is about n log log n, which is almost linear and much less than testing every number by trial division (about n * sqrt(n)). A Uint8Array keeps memory small.
complexity: O(n log log n) time, O(n) space
followups: How would you use a segmented sieve to count primes in [lo, hi] when hi is huge?
Can you cut memory in half by storing odd numbers only?
Why can the inner loop start at i * i?

title: Ugly Number II
statement: An ugly number is a positive integer whose only prime factors are 2, 3 and 5 (1 counts as ugly). The sequence starts 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 8, 9, 10, 12, ... Given n, return the n-th ugly number (1-indexed). Input: n from 1 to 1690. Output: the n-th ugly number.
