hint: Every ugly number after 1 is a smaller ugly number times 2, 3 or 5. Keep three pointers into the list you are building.
approach: Build the sequence in order. Every ugly number except 1 equals some earlier ugly number multiplied by 2, 3 or 5. Keep a list u of the ugly numbers found so far, and three pointers i2, i3, i5 pointing to the next entry that still needs to be multiplied by 2, 3 and 5. The next ugly number is the smallest of u[i2] * 2, u[i3] * 3 and u[i5] * 5. After choosing it, advance every pointer whose product equals the chosen value (several can tie, such as 6 = 2 * 3 = 3 * 2), so duplicates are never added. Because the three streams of candidates are each sorted, taking the minimum each time produces the sequence in increasing order, with n steps of constant work.
followups: How would you do it with a min-heap and a set? Compare the cost.
How does the solution change for primes {2, 7, 13, 19} (Super Ugly Number)?
How would you test whether a single number is ugly?

title: Fraction to Recurring Decimal
statement: Given two integers, numerator and denominator, return the fraction as a decimal string. If the fractional part repeats, put the repeating digits in parentheses. For example 1/3 is "0.(3)" and 1/6 is "0.1(6)". Whole results have no decimal point. Negative results start with "-". Input: numerator and denominator are 32-bit signed integers and the denominator is not 0. Output: the string.
hint: Do long division. The digits start repeating when you see the same remainder again, so remember where each remainder first appeared.
approach: First handle the sign: the result is negative if exactly one input is negative, then work with absolute values. The integer part is the quotient of the division. If the remainder is 0, we are done. Otherwise write a decimal point and continue long division: multiply the remainder by 10, the next digit is the quotient by the denominator, and the new remainder is what is left. Store each remainder in a map with the position in the output where its digit will be written. If a remainder appears again, the digits since its first appearance repeat forever, so insert "(" at the saved position and add ")" at the end. Since the remainder is always less than the denominator, there are at most denominator distinct remainders, so the loop must end.
complexity: O(denominator) time and space in the worst case
followups: Why does the loop always end?
How long can the repeating part be at most?
How would you do the reverse: convert "0.1(6)" to a fraction?

title: Excel Sheet Column Title
statement: Spreadsheet columns are named A, B, ..., Z, AA, AB, ..., AZ, BA, ..., ZZ, AAA, and so on. Given a positive column number, return its title. For example 1 -> "A", 26 -> "Z", 27 -> "AA", 701 -> "ZY". Input: columnNumber from 1 to 2^31 - 1. Output: the title string.
hint: It is like base 26, but digits run from 1 to 26 instead of 0 to 25. Subtract 1 before each division.
approach: This is a base-26 conversion with no zero digit: A is 1 and Z is 26. In normal base 26, we take number % 26 as the last digit and divide by 26. Here the digits are shifted by one, so first subtract 1 from the number: then (number - 1) % 26 is a value from 0 to 25 that maps directly to a letter A to Z, and (number - 1) divided by 26 (rounded down) becomes the new number. We repeat while the number is positive, adding each letter in front of the result (or collecting them and reversing at the end). For 27, subtract 1 to get 26, the letter is 26 % 26 = 0 -> A, next number is 1 -> A, so we get "AA". The loop runs about log base 26 of the input times.
complexity: O(log n) time, O(log n) space
followups: How do you convert a title back to a number?
Why is this not a plain base-26 conversion?
What would change if the sheet used columns starting from 0?

title: Robot Bounded In Circle
statement: A robot starts at (0, 0) facing north. It reads a string of instructions: "G" moves one step forward, "L" turns 90 degrees left, "R" turns 90 degrees right. It repeats the whole instruction string forever. Return true if there is a circle in the plane such that the robot never leaves it, otherwise false. Input: a string of 1 to 100 characters from G, L, R. Output: true or false.
hint: Run the instructions once. Where the robot ends up (position and direction) tells you everything.
approach: Simulate one pass of the instructions, tracking the position and the direction (as an index 0..3 for north, east, south, west). After one pass there are two cases. If the robot is back at the origin, it will repeat the same loop forever, so it is bounded. If it is not at the origin but is facing a different direction than north, then after at most four passes it will have turned a full circle (the turns add up to 360 degrees), and the four displacement vectors rotated by 90 degrees each cancel out, so it returns to the origin and is bounded. Only if the robot is away from the origin and still faces north does every pass add the same displacement, so it drifts away forever and the answer is false.
followups: What if the string is repeated only k times?
Why is four passes always enough to decide?
How would you handle obstacles on the plane?

title: Zigzag Conversion
statement: Write the string s in a zigzag pattern on numRows rows: go down the rows one character at a time, then diagonally up until the top row, and repeat. Then read the rows one by one from top to bottom and join them into a new string. For example, "PAYPALISHIRING" with 3 rows is written as P A H N / A P L S I I G / Y I R and reads "PAHNAPLSIIGYIR". Input: s of length 1 to 1000 and numRows from 1 to 1000. Output: the converted string.
hint: Keep one string builder per row and a direction that flips at the first and last row.
approach: Simulate the writing. Create one list of characters for each row, start on row 0 and move down. For each character of s, append it to the current row, then move to the next row. When the current row is the last row, the direction becomes up; when it is the top row, the direction becomes down. After all characters are placed, join the rows from top to bottom. If numRows is 1 (or at least the length of s) the zigzag never turns, so the string stays the same, and we return it early to avoid a bad direction change. Each character is placed once, so the work is linear. There is also a formula that jumps between characters in each row using the cycle length 2 * numRows - 2, but the simulation is easier to get right.
followups: Can you compute the index of each output character directly, without rows?
How would you invert the conversion?
What if the zigzag were written in columns of a fixed width instead?

title: Text Justification
statement: Format a list of words into lines of exactly maxWidth characters. Pack as many words as fit on each line (words are separated by at least one space). Distribute the extra spaces between the words as evenly as possible; if they do not divide evenly, the gaps on the left get one more space than the gaps on the right. A line with a single word, and the last line, are left-justified: words separated by a single space and padded with spaces on the right. Input: words (1 to 300, each length 1..maxWidth) and maxWidth (1..100). Output: the list of lines.
hint: First find how many words fit on the line. Then compute the spaces: base = spaces / gaps, and the first spaces % gaps gaps get one extra.
approach: Process the words greedily line by line. For the line that starts at word i, keep adding words while the total length of the words plus one space between each pair still fits within maxWidth. Let the chosen words be i..j-1. If this is the last line, or the line has only one word, join the words with a single space and pad the right with spaces. Otherwise, the number of spaces to place is maxWidth minus the total letters, and there are (count - 1) gaps. Each gap gets floor(spaces / gaps), and the leftmost (spaces % gaps) gaps get one more space. Build the line, store it and continue from word j. The greedy choice is forced by the problem (pack as many as fit), so there is nothing to search; the difficulty is the careful handling of the edge rules.
complexity: O(total characters) time, O(total characters) space
followups: How would you minimise the total raggedness (as in TeX) instead of packing greedily?
What if words could be longer than maxWidth and had to be hyphenated?
How would you also centre the last line?

title: Integer to Roman
statement: Convert a positive integer to a Roman numeral. Symbols: I=1, V=5, X=10, L=50, C=100, D=500, M=1000. Subtractive forms are used for 4 (IV), 9 (IX), 40 (XL), 90 (XC), 400 (CD) and 900 (CM). A symbol is never repeated more than three times in a row. Input: an integer from 1 to 3999. Output: the Roman numeral string.
hint: Include the six subtractive pairs in your value table. Then repeatedly take the largest value that fits.
approach: Make a table of values from large to small that includes the subtractive pairs: 1000 M, 900 CM, 500 D, 400 CD, 100 C, 90 XC, 50 L, 40 XL, 10 X, 9 IX, 5 V, 4 IV, 1 I. Walk through the table from the top. While the remaining number is at least the current value, append its symbol and subtract the value. Moving to the next row once the number is smaller than that value ensures that the greedy choice is always the largest possible. This works because the Roman system is built so that the largest-first choice produces the standard form; adding the subtractive pairs as their own rows ensures that 4, 9, 40, 90, 400 and 900 are written correctly instead of as IIII or VIIII. The table has only 13 rows, so the work is constant.
followups: How would you convert Roman numerals back to integers?
Can you do it with lookup arrays for each decimal digit instead of a loop?
How would you validate that a string is a correct Roman numeral?

title: Contains Duplicate
statement: Given an integer array nums, return true if some value appears at least twice, and false if all values are distinct. Input: nums with 0 to 100000 integers in -1e9..1e9. Output: true or false.
hint: As you scan, ask: have I already seen this value?
approach: Keep a hash set of the values seen so far. For each number, check whether it is already in the set. If it is, we have found a duplicate and can return true immediately. If not, add it and continue. After the whole array has been scanned without a repeat, all values are distinct, so return false. A set answers "is it present" in constant time on average, so the total work is linear. The alternatives are comparing every pair, which is quadratic, or sorting and comparing neighbours, which takes O(n log n) time but no extra memory. A quick shortcut is to compare the size of the set made from the array with the array length.
followups: How would you do it in O(1) extra space? What do you give up?
What if you must find a duplicate within a distance k of each other?
What if the array does not fit in memory?

title: Valid Anagram
statement: Given two strings s and t, return true if t is an anagram of s: it uses exactly the same characters with the same counts, in any order. Input: two strings of length 0 to 50000, made of lowercase English letters. Output: true or false.
hint: Two strings are anagrams exactly when every character has the same count in both.
approach: If the lengths differ, the strings cannot be anagrams, so return false. Otherwise count the letters. Use an array of 26 counters (one per lowercase letter). For every character of s add one to its counter, and for every character of t subtract one. If t uses exactly the same letters as s, all counters end at zero; any non-zero counter means that some letter appears a different number of times. We can also stop early: when a counter becomes negative while processing t, t has more of that letter than s. Sorting both strings and comparing also works but costs O(n log n). For Unicode input, replace the array with a hash map from character to count, with the same logic.
followups: What if the inputs contain Unicode characters?
How would you group a whole list of words into anagram classes (Group Anagrams)?
Can you check it with a single pass over both strings?

title: Encode and Decode Strings
statement: Design a way to turn a list of strings into one single string (encode) and turn that string back into the original list (decode). The strings may contain any characters, including digits, separators and the empty string, and the list itself may be empty. For this exercise write codec(strs): build the encoded string, decode it, and return the decoded list. The tests check that the round trip returns exactly the input. Input: up to 200 strings, each up to 200 characters. Output: the decoded list.
hint: A separator character can appear inside a string. Write the length of each string before it, so you never need to guess where it ends.
approach: Use length-prefixed encoding: for each string write its length, then a delimiter such as "#", then the string itself. For example ["ab", ""] becomes "2#ab0#". To decode, start at position 0 and read digits up to the next "#" to get the length n. The next n characters are the string, no matter what they contain, so a "#" or digit inside the data cannot confuse the parser. Jump past those n characters and repeat until the end of the encoded string. A list with one empty string encodes as "0#", while an empty list encodes as "", so the two cases stay distinct. Escaping a separator would also work, but it makes the data longer and the code more error-prone than the length prefix.
followups: How would you do it with escaping instead of length prefixes?
How would you make the encoding streamable, so the decoder needs no knowledge of the total size?
What if the strings can contain any byte, not only text?

title: Missing Number
statement: You are given an array of n distinct integers taken from the range 0..n, so exactly one number from that range is missing. Return the missing number. Input: nums with n elements, 1 <= n <= 10000. Output: the missing number.
hint: You know what the sum of 0..n should be.
approach: The numbers 0 to n add up to n * (n + 1) / 2. The array contains all of them except one, so the real sum of the array is smaller by exactly the missing number. Compute the expected sum with the formula, subtract the actual sum of the array, and the difference is the answer. This uses one pass and constant memory. In languages with fixed-size integers the sum can overflow for large n; XOR avoids this: XOR together all indices 0..n and all array values, and every number that appears twice cancels out, leaving only the missing one. A hash set also works but needs O(n) extra space, and sorting needs O(n log n) time. The formula and the XOR version both need no extra memory.
followups: Solve it with XOR. Why does it avoid overflow?
What if two numbers are missing?
What if the array is sorted? Can you do better than O(n)?
